step_1_3.once_user_provides_story:
Once user provides story + duration + genre, DO NOT just "enhance" it.
Use the STORY ENGINE: a structured system that builds the story
layer by layer.
step_1_3.the_story_engine_6:
THE STORY ENGINE — 6 LAYERS:
LAYER 1: CONCEPT CORE (What is this story REALLY about?)
LAYER 2: CHARACTER ARCHITECTURE (Who changes and why?)
LAYER 3: WORLD RULES (What's normal, what's special?)
LAYER 4: PLOT STRUCTURE (Genre-specific beat sheet)
LAYER 5: EMOTIONAL MAP (What should viewer feel when?)
LAYER 6: HOOK & RETENTION (Why watch? Why KEEP watching?)
Build ALL 6 layers BEFORE writing any scenes!
step_1_3.layer_1_concept_core:
LAYER 1: CONCEPT CORE
Before writing a single scene, answer these:
step_1_3.1_logline_1_sentence:
1. LOGLINE (1 sentence that sells the story):
 Format: "When [PROTAGONIST] discovers [INCITING INCIDENT],
 they must [GOAL] before [STAKES/DEADLINE], but [OBSTACLE]
 stands in the way."

 Example: "When 22-year-old Zain discovers his dead grandfather's
 coded diary, he must decode it within 3 days before the family
 sells the haveli — but someone else is already looking for
 what's hidden inside."
step_1_3.2_theme_the_deeper:
2. THEME (The deeper meaning — shown through ACTION, not dialogue):
 What is this story SAYING about life?
 Theme is NOT stated out loud — it's SHOWN through choices.

 Example: "Knowledge is both a gift and a burden" — shown when
 Zain learns the truth but realizes knowing it puts people in danger.
step_1_3.3_the_promise_what:
3. THE PROMISE (What does the audience EXPECT to get?):
 Mystery → a satisfying reveal
 Thriller → escalating tension + payoff
 Drama → emotional catharsis
 Action → exciting set pieces
 Horror → genuine dread + survival

 YOUR STORY'S PROMISE: ____________________
step_1_3.layer_2_character_architecture:
LAYER 2: CHARACTER ARCHITECTURE
EVERY main character needs a CHARACTER BLUEPRINT:
step_1_3.character_blueprint_name:
CHARACTER BLUEPRINT — [NAME]
IDENTITY:
Name: ____________ Age: ____ Role: ______________
Background: (2-3 sentences — where from, what life is like)
THE TWO GOALS (This is what drives the story):
EXTERNAL Goal: What they WANT (find the treasure, solve
the mystery, save someone) — this is what the PLOT is
INTERNAL Goal: What they NEED (courage, forgiveness,
self-worth, letting go) — this is what the THEME is
FLAW: What's holding them back? (fear, pride, grief,
distrust, guilt) — this creates CONFLICT
ARC: How do they CHANGE?
START state: [who they are at the beginning]
MIDPOINT state: [who they become when challenged]
END state: [who they are after transformation]
VOICE: How do they TALK?
Speech pattern: (formal/casual/slang/quiet/loud)
Favorite words: ("yaar", "actually", "dekh na")
How they show emotion: (hides it / explodes / jokes)
Sample line ONLY they would say: "_______________"
step_1_3.visual_identity_for_phase:
VISUAL IDENTITY (for Phase 3 reference generation):
Build: [Athletic/Heavy/Lean/Slim/Imposing]
Face type: [Sharp/Round/Angular/Soft/Rugged]
Facial hair: [Clean/Stubble/Short beard/Full beard/Mustache]
Signature clothing color: [for instant identification]
One unique physical trait: [scar/glasses/hairstyle/height]
Attractiveness tier: [Hero(Tier1)/Support(Tier2)/Villain(3)]
RELATIONSHIPS:
[Character X]: [dynamic — trust/conflict/mentor/rival]
[Character Y]: [dynamic]
step_1_3.why_this_matters:
WHY THIS MATTERS:
- Without EXTERNAL goal → no plot (nothing happens)
- Without INTERNAL goal → no depth (viewer doesn't care)
- Without FLAW → no arc (character is already perfect = boring)
- Without VOICE → all characters sound the same
step_1_3.example_zain:
EXAMPLE — ZAIN:
CHARACTER BLUEPRINT — ZAIN
IDENTITY:
Name: Zain Age: 22 Role: Protagonist
Background: Final year university student in Faisalabad.
Lives with his mother since his father died. His grandfather
(Danish Sahab) was a famous scholar who disappeared 5 years
ago. Zain never cared about his grandfather's work until now.
EXTERNAL Goal: Find what his grandfather hid before the
family sells the haveli in 3 days.
INTERNAL Goal: Connect with his grandfather's legacy and
find purpose beyond his aimless life.
FLAW: Avoidance — runs from responsibility, takes shortcuts,
never commits to anything. This is why he ignored his
grandfather for years.
ARC:
START: Careless, dismissive ("Dada ki purani kitabein,
kya farak padta hai")
MIDPOINT: Curious but scared (realizes the secret is
dangerous, wants to quit but can't)
END: Committed, changed ("Main nahi rukuunga. Dada ne
yeh mujhe saunpa hai.")
VOICE:
Speech: Casual, modern Urdu, uses English words mixed in
Favorite words: "yaar", "seriously?", "chal chor"
Emotion: Hides behind humor, gets serious only when cornered
Sample line: "Yaar main ne kaha tha na, mujhe ghosts se
allergy hai. Phir bhi le aaye."
RELATIONSHIPS:
Hamza (friend): Comic relief + loyalty, pushes Zain forward
Ayaan (friend): Voice of reason, questions everything
Danish Sahab (grandfather): Absent mentor, mystery source
Naeem (antagonist): Unknown threat, connected to past
step_1_3.create_a_character_blueprint:
Create a CHARACTER BLUEPRINT for EVERY character who:
- Has dialogue
- Appears in 3+ scenes
- Has any impact on the plot
step_1_3.supporting_characters_12_scenes:
Supporting characters (1-2 scenes, no dialogue) don't need full
blueprints — just name, role, and appearance notes.
step_1_3.layer_3_world_rules:
LAYER 3: WORLD RULES
Every story exists in a WORLD with rules. Define them:
step_1_3.world_bible_fill_this:
WORLD BIBLE (fill this out):
WORLD BIBLE — [STORY NAME]
TIME: When does this story take place?
[Exact year/era, or "modern day Faisalabad"]
PLACE: Where? Be specific.
[City, neighborhood, specific buildings]
WHAT'S NORMAL: What does everyday life look like here?
[How people dress, talk, work, commute]
WHAT'S SPECIAL: What makes THIS story's world different?
[The secret, the supernatural element, the hidden history]
RULES OF THE SPECIAL:
If supernatural — what CAN it do? What CAN'T it do?
If mystery — what is known? What is hidden? By who?
If historical — what real events shape this story?
TONE: How does this world FEEL?
[Gritty and real? Magical and warm? Cold and threatening?]
KEY LOCATIONS (list all, with brief vibe):
1. [Location] — [what it feels like, what happens here]
2. [Location] — [vibe, purpose in story]
3. ...
TIMELINE: Key events in chronological order
[PAST events that matter to the story]
[PRESENT events (the actual story)]
[If applicable: FUTURE implications]
step_1_3.why_world_rules_matter:
WHY WORLD RULES MATTER:
- Without timeline → plot holes ("How did he get there so fast?")
- Without location clarity → inconsistent visuals
- Without "rules of special" → magic/mystery feels random
- Without "what's normal" → audience can't tell what's unusual
step_1_3.layer_4_plot_structure: LAYER 4: PLOT STRUCTURE — Genre-Specific Beat Sheets
step_1_3.use_the_beat_sheet:
Use the beat sheet that matches user's genre.
Each beat = approximately 1 scene (adjust for duration).
step_1_3.beat_1_the_hook:
Beat 1 — THE HOOK (Scene 1):
Something strange happens. A body, a disappearance, a discovery.
NOT explanation — pure EVENT. Audience asks "What happened?"
step_1_3.beat_2_the_world:
Beat 2 — THE WORLD BEFORE (Scene 2):
Show protagonist's NORMAL life. Establish what they stand to lose.
Plant 1-2 details that will matter later (audience won't notice yet).
step_1_3.beat_3_the_catalyst:
Beat 3 — THE CATALYST (Scene 3):
Protagonist is PULLED into the mystery. Not by choice — by
circumstance. Something forces them to investigate.
step_1_3.beat_4_investigation_begins:
Beat 4 — INVESTIGATION BEGINS (Scene 4-5):
First clues found. Each clue opens MORE questions (open loops).
Introduce the WRONG THEORY — let audience believe it temporarily.
step_1_3.beat_5_the_first:
Beat 5 — THE FIRST REVELATION (Scene 6):
A clue changes everything. What they thought was happening ISN'T.
The mystery is DEEPER and more DANGEROUS than expected.
step_1_3.beat_6_the_stakes:
Beat 6 — THE STAKES RISE (Scene 7):
Someone gets hurt, something gets stolen, a deadline appears.
The protagonist can't walk away anymore — it's personal now.
step_1_3.beat_7_the_false:
Beat 7 — THE FALSE LEAD (Scene 8):
They follow a clue that leads to a dead end or trap.
This is where the WRONG THEORY collapses.
step_1_3.beat_8_the_dark:
Beat 8 — THE DARK MOMENT (Scene 9):
Lowest point. A betrayal, a loss, or a terrifying discovery.
Protagonist wants to quit. Their FLAW is fully exposed.
step_1_3.beat_9_the_key:
Beat 9 — THE KEY (Scene 10):
One detail they overlooked suddenly clicks. Everything connects.
This is the "AHA!" moment — but now they must ACT.
step_1_3.beat_10_the_confrontation:
Beat 10 — THE CONFRONTATION (Scene 11):
Face the truth, face the antagonist, face the danger.
The protagonist must overcome their FLAW to succeed.
step_1_3.beat_11_the_reveal:
Beat 11 — THE REVEAL (Scene 12):
The full truth revealed. Audience's questions answered.
Should be SURPRISING but make sense when you look back.
step_1_3.beat_12_the_new:
Beat 12 — THE NEW NORMAL (Scene 13):
How has the world changed? How has the protagonist changed?
Leave ONE small question unanswered (sequel potential / lingering mystery).
step_1_3.beat_1_the_moment:
Beat 1 — THE MOMENT (Scene 1):
Start with a PIVOTAL emotional moment (not the beginning of time).
A funeral, a goodbye, a discovery, a return home.
step_1_3.beat_2_the_weight:
Beat 2 — THE WEIGHT (Scene 2):
Show what this moment COSTS the protagonist emotionally.
Their daily life, their relationships, their struggle.
step_1_3.beat_3_the_trigger:
Beat 3 — THE TRIGGER (Scene 3):
Something forces them to confront what they've been avoiding.
A letter, a person returning, a deadline, a crisis.
step_1_3.beat_4_the_attempt:
Beat 4 — THE ATTEMPT (Scene 4-5):
Protagonist tries to deal with it their OLD way (using their flaw).
It doesn't work. Things get worse.
step_1_3.beat_5_the_connection:
Beat 5 — THE CONNECTION (Scene 6):
A relationship moment — someone sees through the protagonist's
walls. A vulnerable conversation. Trust begins to form.
step_1_3.beat_6_the_setback:
Beat 6 — THE SETBACK (Scene 7):
The protagonist's flaw causes real damage to a relationship
or situation. They hurt someone they care about.
step_1_3.beat_7_the_reflection:
Beat 7 — THE REFLECTION (Scene 8):
Alone, processing. A memory, a realization, a quiet moment
where change becomes possible.
step_1_3.beat_8_the_choice:
Beat 8 — THE CHOICE (Scene 9):
Protagonist must choose between their old self and growth.
This choice costs them something real.
step_1_3.beat_9_the_action:
Beat 9 — THE ACTION (Scene 10):
They act on their choice. It's hard, it's scary, but they do it.
This demonstrates the internal transformation.
step_1_3.beat_10_the_resolution:
Beat 10 — THE RESOLUTION (Scene 11-12):
Relationships heal or change. The world is different.
Not necessarily "happy" — but MEANINGFUL. The protagonist
is a different person than they were in Scene 1.
step_1_3.beat_1_the_bang:
Beat 1 — THE BANG (Scene 1):
Open with ACTION. A chase, a fight, an escape, a disaster.
Show the protagonist's SKILLS in action. Hook immediately.
step_1_3.beat_2_the_mission:
Beat 2 — THE MISSION (Scene 2):
What must be done? Why? What happens if they fail?
Clear EXTERNAL goal with a DEADLINE.
step_1_3.beat_3_the_team:
Beat 3 — THE TEAM (Scene 3):
Assemble the crew / meet the allies. Each has a specific skill.
Establish dynamics (leader, comic relief, expert, wildcard).
step_1_3.beat_4_the_journey:
Beat 4 — THE JOURNEY BEGINS (Scene 4):
First obstacle. They overcome it — but it costs something.
Establishes the DIFFICULTY level of the mission.
step_1_3.beat_5_the_escalation:
Beat 5 — THE ESCALATION (Scene 5-6):
Each scene is harder than the last. New obstacles, new enemies.
One team member gets hurt or fails — stakes feel REAL.
step_1_3.beat_6_the_betrayal:
Beat 6 — THE BETRAYAL / TWIST (Scene 7):
Something they trusted turns against them. An ally betrays,
a plan fails, the enemy was closer than they thought.
step_1_3.beat_7_the_low:
Beat 7 — THE LOW POINT (Scene 8):
They lose. Badly. Resources gone, team scattered.
Protagonist must dig deep — internal flaw confronted.
step_1_3.beat_8_the_rally:
Beat 8 — THE RALLY (Scene 9):
Protagonist finds inner strength. New plan. Creative solution.
The flaw is overcome — this enables the final push.
step_1_3.beat_9_the_final:
Beat 9 — THE FINAL BATTLE (Scene 10-11):
Everything on the line. The biggest set piece.
Every character contributes their unique skill.
step_1_3.beat_10_the_aftermath:
Beat 10 — THE AFTERMATH (Scene 12):
Mission complete (or failed with meaning). What was the cost?
How are they changed? What comes next?
step_1_3.beat_1_the_warning:
Beat 1 — THE WARNING (Scene 1):
Something wrong is shown BEFORE the protagonist arrives.
A death, a symbol, a disturbing image. Plant the seed.
step_1_3.beat_2_the_arrival:
Beat 2 — THE ARRIVAL (Scene 2):
Protagonist enters the dangerous space — but doesn't know yet.
Everything seems fine. Audience knows better (dramatic irony).
step_1_3.beat_3_the_first:
Beat 3 — THE FIRST SIGN (Scene 3):
Something small but wrong. A sound, a shadow, a missing object.
Protagonist dismisses it. Audience leans in.
step_1_3.beat_4_the_denial:
Beat 4 — THE DENIAL (Scene 4):
More signs. Protagonist rationalizes. "Hawaa thi", "Khayal tha".
But the audience sees what they don't.
step_1_3.beat_5_the_proof:
Beat 5 — THE PROOF (Scene 5-6):
Undeniable evidence. Something happens that CAN'T be explained.
Protagonist's world cracks — fear begins.
step_1_3.beat_6_the_research:
Beat 6 — THE RESEARCH (Scene 7):
They investigate the history. What happened here before?
Each answer makes it WORSE. The threat has RULES.
step_1_3.beat_7_the_attack:
Beat 7 — THE ATTACK (Scene 8):
The threat becomes direct and physical. Someone gets hurt.
Protagonist realizes — they can't just leave.
step_1_3.beat_8_the_darkest:
Beat 8 — THE DARKEST POINT (Scene 9):
Trapped. Alone. The threat is overwhelming.
Psychological horror: their own fear/guilt used against them.
step_1_3.beat_9_the_fight:
Beat 9 — THE FIGHT BACK (Scene 10):
Protagonist uses what they learned in "research" to fight.
But the rules have a cost — sacrifice required.
step_1_3.beat_10_the_survival:
Beat 10 — THE SURVIVAL (Scene 11-12):
They escape/defeat the threat — but are forever changed.
End with ONE lingering sign that it's not truly over.
step_1_3.beat_1_the_era:
Beat 1 — THE ERA (Scene 1):
Establish time period with SPECIFIC date and event.
"14 November 1857, Srinagar. Angrezon ki fauj 2 ghante door thi."
NOT vague history — A specific MOMENT.
step_1_3.beat_2_the_people:
Beat 2 — THE PEOPLE (Scene 2):
Show daily life in this era. How people dress, work, pray.
Ground the audience in THIS world before the drama starts.
step_1_3.beat_3_the_disruption:
Beat 3 — THE DISRUPTION (Scene 3):
An event shatters normal life. War arrives, a ruler falls,
a secret is discovered, an injustice occurs.
step_1_3.beat_4_the_choice:
Beat 4 — THE CHOICE (Scene 4-5):
Protagonist must choose a side. Loyalty vs survival.
Duty vs family. Truth vs safety.
step_1_3.beat_5_the_struggle:
Beat 5 — THE STRUGGLE (Scene 6-7):
Living with the consequences of the choice.
Show the HUMAN cost of historical events through one person's eyes.
step_1_3.beat_6_the_sacrifice:
Beat 6 — THE SACRIFICE (Scene 8-9):
Something precious is lost. A life, a home, a relationship.
Make it PERSONAL, not just "many people died."
step_1_3.beat_7_the_legacy:
Beat 7 — THE LEGACY (Scene 10-11):
What they protected/created/saved lives on.
Jump to present day or show the long-term impact.
step_1_3.beat_8_the_echo:
Beat 8 — THE ECHO (Scene 12):
The past connects to the present. A descendant finds something.
A secret surfaces. The story is not finished.
step_1_3.note_historical_stories_often:
NOTE: Historical stories often use DUAL TIMELINES:
- PAST: Where the drama happened
- PRESENT: Where someone discovers the past
Cut between them to build mystery and emotional connection.
step_1_3.layer_5_emotional_map:
LAYER 5: EMOTIONAL MAP
Map what the VIEWER should feel in each scene:
step_1_3.emotional_map_format:
EMOTIONAL MAP FORMAT:
Scene | Viewer Emotion | How We Create It
1 | Intrigue/Shock | Visual hook + mystery setup
2 | Comfort/Curiosity | Normal world + planted clues
3 | Excitement/Worry | Catalyst event + stakes
4 | Tension/Discovery | Investigation + clues
5 | Surprise | First twist/revelation
6 | Fear/Urgency | Stakes rise + danger
7 | Frustration/Hope | False lead + new direction
8 | Despair/Empathy | Dark moment + vulnerability
9 | Excitement/Awe | Key discovery + rally
10 | Tension/Edge | Climax confrontation
11 | Relief/Wonder | Reveal + resolution
12 | Satisfaction+Itch | New normal + lingering Q
step_1_3.rules:
RULES:
- NEVER two scenes with the same emotion back-to-back
- After HIGH tension → give a BREATHING scene (but with a hook)
- After SADNESS → give a WARM moment before dropping again
- The emotional PEAK should be in the last 1/3 of the video
- End on an emotion that makes them want MORE
step_1_3.the_hook_first_30:
THE HOOK (First 30 seconds = Life or Death):
FIRST 30 SECONDS MUST CONTAIN:
0-6 sec: VISUAL STUN — arresting image/action
(NOT misty mountains. NOT philosophy.)
Running, fire, blood, impact, explosion, hiding.
6-15 sec: QUESTION PLANT — viewer MUST ask "What's going on?"
A mystery, a chase, an unexplained event.
15-30 sec: STAKES CLEAR — why should I CARE?
Someone is in danger. Something will be lost.
A deadline exists. Lives are at stake.
BANNED from first 30 seconds:
Philosophy ("Log kehte hain...")
Slow nature shots (mountains, rivers, sunrise)
Characters sitting and talking
World-building exposition
Narrator explaining background
step_1_3.retention_open_loops_system:
RETENTION — OPEN LOOPS SYSTEM:
An OPEN LOOP is an unanswered question in the viewer's mind.
As long as loops are open, they CANNOT stop watching.
step_1_3.open_loops_rules:
OPEN LOOPS RULES:
1. Scene 1 opens at least 1 STRONG loop (the central mystery)
2. Each scene either opens OR closes a loop (or both)
3. NEVER close a loop without opening a new one (until the end)
4. Maximum 3 loops open at the same time (more = confusing)
5. Close ALL loops by the climax (except 1 for sequel potential)
step_1_3.open_loops_map_create:
OPEN LOOPS MAP (Create this for your story):
Loop # | Question | Opened | Closed
1 | "Kitaab mein kya hai?" | Scene 1 | Scene 10
2 | "Dada kahan gaye?" | Scene 2 | Scene 11
3 | "Naeem kaun hai?" | Scene 4 | Scene 9
4 | "Chabi kiska hai?" | Scene 5 | Scene 8

2. SPECIFY exact filename to attach

step_3_0g.step_30g_character_timeline_system:
Step 3.0G: CHARACTER TIMELINE SYSTEM (NEW — CRITICAL!)
Characters are NOT static! They change through the story.
Their APPEARANCE changes with the story. Plan for this!

THE PROBLEM WITH ONE REFERENCE IMAGE:
You generate 1 character reference at the start.
But by Scene 8, the character has been:
- In a fight (wounds, torn clothes)
- Traveling for days (dirt, sweat, stubble)
- Emotionally broken (different posture, expression)
- In a different time period (younger/older version)

If you use the SAME clean reference for Scene 8 → inconsistency!
The character should look ROUGH by now, but your reference shows
them CLEAN.
step_3_0g.solution_character_state_timeline:
SOLUTION: CHARACTER STATE TIMELINE

For each main character, create a STATE TIMELINE that maps their
appearance changes across the story:

CHARACTER STATE TIMELINE — [NAME]
Scenes | STATE Name | Appearance Changes
1-3 | STATE A: Clean | Default look. Clean clothes,
fresh face, no injuries.
REF: CHAR_[Name]_StateA_ref.png
4-6 | STATE B: Alert | Same clothes but slightly dusty.
More serious expression default.
Hair less neat.
REF: CHAR_[Name]_StateB_ref.png
7-9 | STATE C: Rough | Torn jacket sleeve (left arm).
Cut on right cheek (from Scene 6).
Dirt on face and clothes.
Exhausted eyes.
REF: CHAR_[Name]_StateC_ref.png
10-12 | STATE D: Final | Same injuries but bandaged cheek.
New determination in eyes.
Standing taller despite wounds.
REF: CHAR_[Name]_StateD_ref.png

HOW TO USE THIS:
1. Generate reference images for StateA ONLY at project start
2. Generate StateB/C/D ONLY when story demands it (on-demand)
3. In each scene, use the CORRECT state's reference image
4. Injuries/changes ACCUMULATE — they don't reset between scenes!


CHARACTER STATE EVOLUTION RULES (CRITICAL!):
NEVER generate StateB/C/D independently!
ALWAYS derive from StateA reference image!
StateA = ONLY state generated from scratch (no ref)
StateB = ATTACH StateA + describe ONLY changes
StateC = ATTACH StateA + describe accumulated changes
StateD = ATTACH StateA + describe all accumulated changes
ALWAYS use StateA as base — NEVER derive StateC from
StateB (face will DRIFT away from original!)
step_3_0g.rule_1_statea_only_fresh:
RULE 1: StateA = ONLY fresh generation (no reference needed)
 Generate clean studio portrait from text description only.
 This becomes the PERMANENT face anchor for this character.
step_3_0g.rule_2_statebcd_always_attach:
RULE 2: StateB/C/D = ALWAYS attach StateA as reference
 Prompt format:
 "[CHARACTER REFERENCE: attached image — this is the EXACT 
 same person. Match face, bone structure, skin tone, and 
 all features PRECISELY.]

 CHANGES FROM BASE (ONLY these differences):
 - [list specific changes: dust, wound, torn fabric, etc.]

 Everything NOT listed above remains IDENTICAL to the 
 attached reference."
step_3_0g.rule_3_generate_states_ondemand:
RULE 3: Generate states ON-DEMAND only
WRONG: Generate StateA + StateB + StateC at project start
RIGHT: Generate StateA at start → Generate StateB ONLY 
 when Scene X needs it → Generate StateC ONLY when Scene Y 
 needs it
step_3_0g.rule_4_never_chain_states:
RULE 4: NEVER chain states
WRONG: StateA → StateB → use StateB to make StateC
RIGHT: StateA → StateB (from A) → StateC (from A, NOT B)
 Why: Each generation drifts ~5% from reference. 
 A→B→C = 10% drift. A→C directly = only 5% drift.

Scene 5: Character gets shoulder wound
 → NOW generate StateB: attach [Character]_StateA_ref.png
 → Prompt: "SAME person from attached image. Match face 
 EXACTLY. ONLY changes: shoulder graze on RIGHT shoulder, 
 dried dark blood staining fabric around small tear, 
 expression more tired. Everything else IDENTICAL."
Scene 9: Character more battered
 → NOW generate StateC: attach [Character]_StateA_ref.png (NOT B!)
 → Prompt: "SAME person from attached. ONLY changes: shoulder

ERA AUTHENTICITY LOCK (UNIVERSAL — FOR ANY HISTORICAL PROJECT):
AI DEFAULT = MODERN CLOTHING! You MUST override this!
Without explicit era lock, AI will generate modern items
regardless of what time period you describe.
This happens in EVERY historical era — Mughal, Roman,
Medieval, Victorian, WW2, 1970s — AI defaults to 2024.

HOW TO USE ERA LOCK:
At the START of your project, define your era with:

1. ERA DEFINITION BLOCK (add to project config):
"HISTORICAL ERA: [Exact year/period] [Region/Culture]. 
ALL clothing, grooming, architecture, and accessories MUST 
be authentic to [century] [culture] context."

2. ANTI-MODERN CHECKLIST (customize per era):
List specific modern items that MUST NOT appear. 
AI will sneak these in if not explicitly banned.

3. CORRECT TERMINOLOGY TABLE (customize per era):
Map common modern English words to era-correct terms.
AI interprets "coat" as modern jacket unless you specify.

4. CULTURAL CONFUSION PREVENTION:
Identify cultures AI commonly CONFUSES with your target era.
Explicitly state what your era IS and IS NOT.
step_3_0g.example_1658_mughal_deccan_india:
EXAMPLE — 1658 Mughal Deccan India:

ERA DEFINITION:
"HISTORICAL ERA: 1658 Mughal Deccan India. ALL clothing, 
grooming, and accessories MUST be authentic to 17th century 
Mughal military/travel context."

ANTI-MODERN CHECKLIST:
- NO modern buttons (use fabric ties, hooks, or wraparound)
- NO machine stitching (hand-stitched seams only)
- NO collar shirts or Nehru jackets
- NO cargo pockets or breast pockets
- NO zippers or snaps
- NO synthetic/polyester fabric look
- NO modern fade haircuts or salon-styled hair
- NO shaped beard edges or modern grooming lines
- NO modern belt buckles (use leather tie or fabric wrap)
- NO shoes with rubber soles or modern construction

CORRECT TERMINOLOGY TABLE:
| Wrong Term | Correct Term for This Era |
|----------------|----------------------------------------|
| "vest" | "bandi/sadri" (sleeveless layering |
| | garment, no buttons, fabric ties) |
| "coat" | "angarkha" (wrap-front coat with |
| | diagonal closure, fabric ties at side) |
| "pants" | "churidar" or "shalwar" |
| "belt" | "kamarband" (fabric waist sash) |
| "scarf" | "patka" (Mughal waist/shoulder sash) |
| "turban" | "pagri" (see headwear rules below) |
| "shirt" | "kurta" or "jama" (long tunic) |

CULTURAL CONFUSION PREVENTION:
AI confuses Mughal with Sikh (turban styles)
AI confuses Mughal with Rajput (headwear)
AI confuses Mughal with Japanese (wrap clothing)
For EACH confusion risk, provide explicit "THIS IS / THIS IS NOT"

Generic headwear terms = AI picks WRONG style!
"turban" → AI defaults to Sikh dastar (WRONG for most eras)
"hat" → AI defaults to modern baseball cap or fedora
"crown" → AI defaults to European medieval style
"cap" → AI defaults to modern beanie or snapback
ALWAYS describe headwear with SPECIFIC construction:
Shape, how it sits, what it covers, what it exposes,
fabric wrapping method, decorations, and explicit
"THIS IS NOT: [list wrong styles]"

on head], [what body parts it covers/exposes]. Fabric [how

SYMBOL/MARKING AUTHENTICITY (UNIVERSAL RULE):
AI will interpret symbols as MODERN equivalents!
"crescent + star" → Pakistan/Turkey flag
"cross" → Christian cross (even if decorative)
"eagle" → USA/German symbol
"sun" → Japanese flag
"star" → Star of David or US military star
ALWAYS describe symbols as PHYSICAL OBJECTS, not concepts!

SYMBOL DESCRIPTION TEMPLATE:
"A hand-carved/painted/embossed [physical shape description] 
with [additional elements described by shape, not by name]. 
This is a [FAMILY/CLAN/GUILD] marking, NOT a national flag, 
NOT a religious symbol. The [technique: carving/painting/etc.] 
is [aged/fresh/shallow/deep], [material details].

NOT [flag/symbol AI might confuse it with]
NOT [another symbol AI might confuse it with]"

 small round dots arranged in a triangle below it. This

ANCHOR IMAGE — PURE ENVIRONMENT RULE:
ANCHOR IMAGE = ENVIRONMENT ONLY!
NO characters in anchor
NO story objects (props, weapons, vehicles) in anchor
NO story-specific elements in anchor
Anchor shows ONLY:
- Location (mountain pass, room, street, forest, etc.)
- Lighting setup (practical lights, sun, moon, etc.)
- Color grading (shadow color, highlight color)
- Atmosphere (dust level, fog level, air clarity)
- Time of day (night, dawn, day, dusk)
- Architectural/environmental textures

WHY: If anchor contains characters, other frames will COPY 
those characters' poses and positions (anchor copying problem).
If anchor contains objects, same issue.

ANCHOR PROMPT FORMAT:
"Generate a photorealistic EMPTY environment shot in 16:9. 
NO people. NO characters. NO objects. ONLY the location:
[detailed environment description]
[lighting setup]
[color grading targets]
This will be used as a style/environment reference for all 
other frames in this scene."

THEN for character frames:
Attach: Character ref(s) + Anchor environment
→ Characters come from character refs
→ Environment comes from anchor
→ Each does its own job. No confusion.


MAX REFERENCE IMAGES PER PROMPT:
TESTED AND CONFIRMED:
- 1-3 images: + Gemini handles well, good attention to each
- 4 images: Acceptable but attention starts to spread
- 5+ images: - Attention dilutes, face matching drops
- 10 images: -- TESTED — faces wrong, details ignored

RULE: MAXIMUM 4 reference images per prompt.
Ideal: 2-3 images (character + anchor, or 2 characters + anchor)

If a frame needs more references than 4:
→ Prioritize: Character faces FIRST (face match is hardest)
→ Then: Anchor/environment
→ Describe objects in TEXT instead of attaching object ref
→ Or: Generate in 2 passes (environment first, then add character)


CHARACTER REFERENCE MANDATE (ABSOLUTE RULE!):
NEVER generate a character without their reference
image attached. NO EXCEPTIONS. ZERO TOLERANCE.
If character ref is NOT attached → that character
CANNOT appear in the frame. Period.

THE RULE:
Character MENTIONED in prompt = Character ref MUST be attached.
Character ref NOT attached = Character CANNOT be in frame.

WRONG:
  Attached: Sandook ref + Anchor
  Prompt: "Aurangzaib, Dalawar, Farid, Sikandar walking..."
 Result: 4 RANDOM faces — no consistency!

RIGHT (Option A — attach refs):
  Attached: Aurangzaib ref + Dalawar ref + Anchor
  Prompt: "EXACTLY 2 people: Aurangzaib and Dalawar..."
 Result: Faces match references +

RIGHT (Option B — reduce characters):
  Attached: Anchor only (no character refs available)
  Prompt: "4 distant silhouettes walking, NO readable 
 faces, too far for facial detail..."
 Result: No face matching needed, silhouettes fine +

RIGHT (Option C — split into passes):
 Pass 1: Generate Aurangzaib + Dalawar with their refs
 Pass 2: Generate Farid + Sikandar with their refs
 Composite if needed in post-production

DECISION TREE:
 Character's face READABLE in frame?
 - YES → Character ref MUST be attached
 (if no slot available → remove from frame 
 or make them a background silhouette)
 - NO (distant/silhouette/back turned) 
→ No ref needed, describe by clothing only
→ "A distant figure in dark olive garment"
→ Face must NOT be readable at this distance

SLOT PRIORITY (when limited to 3-4 attachments):
1st priority: Hero/speaking character ref (face MUST match)
2nd priority: 2nd character ref (if face visible)
3rd priority: Anchor/environment ref
4th priority: Object ref (or describe object in text instead)

NEVER sacrifice character ref for object ref — faces matter 
more than objects. Objects can be described in text. 
Faces CANNOT be accurately generated from text alone.

EXCEPTION TO ABOVE: See RECURRING ELEMENT RULE below — 
objects that appear in 2+ frames ALSO need reference images!


RECURRING ELEMENT REFERENCE RULE (UNIVERSAL!):
IF ANY VISUAL ELEMENT APPEARS IN 2+ FRAMES,
IT MUST HAVE A DEDICATED REFERENCE IMAGE!
Text description alone = GUARANTEED inconsistency!
AI generates a NEW version every time from text.
ONLY a reference image locks the design across frames.

THE UNIVERSAL PROBLEM:
You describe "a dark arched wooden door with a padlock" in 
text across 6 clips. Result:
- Clip 1: Round arch, light brown wood, brass padlock
- Clip 2: Pointed arch, dark wood, no padlock visible
- Clip 3: Square door frame, medium wood, steel padlock
- Clip 4: Round arch again but DIFFERENT wood grain
→ Viewer thinks: "Is this even the same location?!"

AI does NOT remember previous generations. Every prompt is 
independent. The ONLY way to get the SAME element across 
frames is to SHOW it the same reference image every time.

THE RULE:
Any visual element that appears in 2 or more frames 
MUST have its own dedicated reference image generated 
BEFORE production begins.

THIS APPLIES TO EVERYTHING:
CATEGORY | EXAMPLES
ARCHITECTURE | Doors, windows, gates, arches,
staircases, corridors, walls,
balconies, rooftops
ROOMS / INTERIORS | Room layout, furniture arrangement,
wall decorations, light fixtures,
floor pattern, ceiling details
EXTERIORS | Streets, lanes, paths, courtyards,
landscapes, building facades
FURNITURE | Tables, chairs, beds, shelves,
desks, cabinets
VEHICLES | Cars, bikes, carts, horses,
boats (if recurring)
WEAPONS / TOOLS | Swords, bows, shields, torches,
tools, walking sticks
PROPS / OBJECTS | Books, letters, boxes, keys, locks,
chains, rings, seals, maps
SIGNAGE / MARKS | Symbols, crests, carvings, signs
(described in text, no readable text)
ENVIRONMENT DETAIL | Specific trees, rock formations,
water features, light fixtures


HOW TO IDENTIFY RECURRING ELEMENTS (PRE-PRODUCTION):
BEFORE generating any scene frames, do this scan:
step_3_0g.step_1_list_every_visual: STEP 1: List every visual element in the scene
step_3_0g.step_2_count_how_many: STEP 2: Count how many frames/clips each element appears in
step_3_0g.step_3_any_element_with: STEP 3: Any element with count 2+ → NEEDS reference image

RECURRING ELEMENT REFERENCE TYPES:

TYPE 1: CLOSE REFERENCE (for objects, props, details)

- Clean background, good lighting, all details visible
- Example: OBJ_HaveliDoor_ref.png — door fills 80% of frame,

- Generate a MACRO close-up of the specific detail

 chain, filling frame, every rust spot and link visible

ATTACHMENT PRIORITY (when slots limited):
When you can only attach 3-4 images, prioritize:

1st: Character face ref (if character face visible)
2nd: KEY recurring element ref (the most prominent one)
3rd: Anchor / environment ref
4th: Secondary recurring element ref

If an element can't be attached due to slot limit:
→ Describe it in text BUT copy the EXACT SAME description 
 word-for-word in every prompt where it appears.
 DO NOT rephrase, DO NOT paraphrase, DO NOT "vary the 
 language." EXACT same text = closest to consistency 
 without a reference image.


CONSISTENCY LOCK PARAGRAPH (for recurring elements):
When a recurring element appears, add this block:

"[ELEMENT] CONSISTENCY LOCK:
This [element] must match the attached [element] reference 
EXACTLY — same shape, same color, same material, same 
damage/wear pattern, same size proportions. 
Do NOT redesign, reimagine, or create a new version.
It must look like the SAME physical [element] photographed 
from a different angle."


PERSPECTIVE & SCALE ACCURACY SYSTEM (CRITICAL!):
AI's #1 VISUAL PROBLEM: Wrong perspective & scale!
When you give AI an object/character reference, it will:
- Make the object GIANT (to "show it off")
- Break camera perspective (walls straight but floor tilted)
- Shrink rooms / environments around the object
- Make characters too big or too small for the space
- Doors, furniture, ceilings become wrong proportions
THIS MUST BE FIXED IN EVERY PROMPT!

THE PROBLEM EXPLAINED:
When you say "envelope on table" + attach envelope reference,
AI thinks: "The envelope is important! Make it BIG so viewer 
can see it clearly!"

Result: Envelope covers 40% of table = looks like a poster
Reality: Envelope should cover 5-8% of table surface

Same with characters: "Put Dalawar in the ghaat pass"
AI makes Dalawar fill 60% of frame height in a wide shot
Reality: At 35 feet camera distance, a person should be 
about 25-30% of frame height

PERSPECTIVE & SCALE RULES (Add to EVERY prompt):

RULE PS1: REAL-WORLD SIZE ANCHORING
Always state REAL physical sizes of objects and spaces:
"An envelope on a table in a room"
"A standard letter envelope (9x4 inches) lies on a 
 wooden table (5 feet x 3 feet) in a room (18x14 feet, 
 12-foot ceiling). The envelope is SMALL relative to the 
 table — covering less than 8% of the table surface."

RULE PS2: CAMERA PERSPECTIVE CONSISTENCY
All elements must obey the SAME camera angle:
"Table seen from above, walls seen from front" (IMPOSSIBLE)
"Camera is at eye level (5.5 feet height), angled slightly 
 downward about 10 degrees. ALL surfaces — floor, walls, 
 ceiling, table, objects — must follow this SINGLE consistent 
 camera perspective with correct vanishing points."

STATE THE CAMERA AS A PHYSICAL POSITION:
"Imagine a real cinematographer standing at [position], 
holding a camera at [height], pointing [direction] with 
[lens]. Everything in the frame must look exactly as this 
real camera would capture it — correct perspective, correct 
relative sizes, correct depth."

RULE PS3: OBJECT-TO-ENVIRONMENT RATIO
Always describe how SMALL the object is relative to its space:
"The sandook is visible on the path" (AI makes it huge)
"The wooden sandook (2.5 feet long, 1.5 feet wide) sits 
 on the stone path (5 feet wide). The sandook takes up 
 about HALF the path width. At camera distance of 18 feet, 
 the sandook should appear as roughly 12% of frame width."

RULE PS4: HUMAN SCALE REFERENCE
Use human body as scale anchor:
- Standard door height: 6.5-7 feet (character should be 
 slightly shorter than doorframe)
- Table height: about waist level (3 feet)
- Chair seat: about knee level (1.5 feet) 
- Ceiling: character height x 1.7 to 2.0 (typical room)
- If character stands next to door, their head should be 
 at about 85-90% of door height

RULE PS5: VANISHING POINT LOCK
Every prompt must specify ONE consistent viewpoint:
"CAMERA POSITION: 
- Height: [X feet from ground]
- Distance: [X feet from main subject] 
- Angle: [eye level / slightly high / slightly low]
- Lens: [wide 24mm / normal 50mm / close 85mm]
- ALL walls, floor, ceiling, furniture, and objects must 
 share the SAME vanishing point(s) consistent with this 
 exact camera position. No mixed perspectives."

RULE PS6: DEPTH SIZE SCALING
Objects further from camera must be proportionally SMALLER:
"A person at 10 feet from camera appears roughly TWICE the 
height of the same person at 20 feet from camera. Objects 
in the background must be noticeably smaller than identical 
objects in the foreground. This is basic perspective — enforce 
it strictly."


PERSPECTIVE FIX TEMPLATE (Add to any prompt with objects):
Add this block to prompts where objects or scale matters:

"SCALE & PERSPECTIVE LOCK:
- Camera position: [height] feet high, [distance] feet from 
 subject, [angle] degrees, [lens]mm lens
- Room/space dimensions: [L x W x H] feet 
- Object real size: [dimensions] — occupies approximately 
 [X%] of frame width at this camera distance
- Human reference: a standing adult (5'8") would reach [X%] 
 of frame height at this distance
- ALL elements must share ONE consistent vanishing point
- Objects further from camera MUST appear proportionally smaller
- Do NOT enlarge any object beyond its real-world size ratio
- Think like a real cinematographer: would this look correct 
 through a real camera at this position? If not, fix it."


COMMON AI SCALE MISTAKES AND FIXES:

MISTAKE: Object reference makes object GIANT
FIX: "The [object] is [real dimensions]. At [camera distance], 
it appears as approximately [X%] of frame width. Do NOT 
enlarge it to fill the frame."

MISTAKE: Room feels like a miniature/dollhouse
FIX: "This is a real [LxWxH] foot room. A 5'8" adult standing 
in the center would have about [X] feet of ceiling clearance 
above their head. The room must feel this spacious."

MISTAKE: Walls and floor have different perspectives
FIX: "Single camera viewpoint. All surfaces obey the SAME 
perspective geometry. If the floor tiles converge toward a 
vanishing point, the wall edges must converge toward the 
same horizon line."

MISTAKE: Door too small / furniture wrong scale
FIX: "Standard interior door: 6.5 feet tall x 2.5 feet wide. 
Table: 3 feet tall. Chair seat: 1.5 feet. All furniture must 
be correctly proportioned to the door and room dimensions."

MISTAKE: Character too big for environment (fills frame in wide shot)
FIX: "At [camera distance] feet with a [lens]mm lens, a 5'8" 
person occupies approximately [X%] of frame height. Character 
must not exceed this proportion."

CORRECT PROMPT FORMAT:
WRONG (State not specified):
"Ayaan looks down at the wrapped leather book in his hands"
(AI assumes: looking at = reading = book OPEN)

CORRECT (State explicitly specified):
"Ayaan holds the ancient leather book in his gloved hands.
The book is CLOSED - he is holding it protectively against
his chest, NOT reading it. The book cover (as shown in 2nd
reference) faces outward, brass clasp visible. He glances
toward his friend off-frame while securing the CLOSED book."


ACTION vs STATE Conflicts:
Some actions IMPLY a state. Be careful!
ACTION → IMPLIED STATE → SPECIFY INSTEAD
"looks at book" → OPEN → "holds CLOSED book, glances at
cover"
"reads the page" → OPEN → (only use if book should be
open)
"examines the book" → OPEN → "examines the CLOSED book's
cover"
"flips through" → OPEN → (only use if book should be
open)
"clutches the book" → CLOSED → good! implies closed
"holds against chest" → CLOSED → good! implies closed
"opens the book" → TRANSITION → describe what's inside when
opened
"looks down at book" → OPEN → "looks down at CLOSED book in
hands"

THE PROBLEM: Even when you say “book is closed” in one part of prompt, if your ACTION
implies OPEN, AI will open it!
CONFLICTING PROMPT:
"He holds the wrapped leather-bound book" ← implies CLOSED
...
"looks down at the book" ← implies READING = OPEN!
...
"Book remains identical (dark leather + brass clasp)"

RESULT: AI opened the book because "looks down at" = reading!

BREATH/FOG/SMOKE EFFECTS (CRITICAL!)
THE PROBLEM: When you mention “visible breath” or “breath in cold air,” AI creates
DRAMATIC DRAGON-LIKE SMOKE that looks completely unnatural!
WHAT AI GENERATES:
- Thick white smoke pouring from mouth
- Fog going in weird directions (toward objects)
- Constant smoke stream like cigarette
- Looks like character is breathing fire (white)
- Unnatural, distracting, breaks immersion!

REAL COLD BREATH looks like:
NATURAL BREATH:
- Very SUBTLE, thin wisp
- Appears briefly on EXHALE only
- Dissipates within 1 second
- Goes slightly downward/forward
- NOT visible on every breath
- Small puff, not smoke stream
step_3_0g.solution_avoid_or_strictly_control:
SOLUTION: Avoid or Strictly Control Breath Effects
OPTION 1: AVOID COMPLETELY (Recommended)
Simply don't mention breath at all!
Most viewers won't notice missing breath vapor.
They WILL notice weird dragon smoke.

Remove: "His breath is visible in the cold"
Remove: "Breath visibly puffs"
Instead: Don't mention breath - focus on other cold indicators
OPTION 2: MINIMAL MENTION (Risky)
If you MUST show breath, be VERY specific:

"A TINY, barely-visible wisp of breath vapor appears
briefly on one exhale - very subtle, thin, and
dissipates immediately. NOT thick smoke, NOT dramatic,
NOT constant. Natural and barely noticeable."

OPTION 3: SHOW COLD WITHOUT BREATH
Better ways to show cold environment:
- Snow on clothing/hair
- Red nose/cheeks
- Character shivering slightly
- Frost on eyelashes/beard
- Hunched posture against cold
- Hands rubbing together
- Snow flakes in air
(None of these create weird effects!)


BREATH EFFECT LOCK:
If scene is in cold environment, add this:
BREATH/FOG LOCK:
 - NO visible breath vapor (or MINIMAL only)
 - NO thick smoke/fog from mouth
 - NO dragon-like breath effects
 - NO constant steam from breathing
 - If any breath shown: tiny wisp, immediately dissipates
 - Show cold through: snow on clothes, red cheeks, shivering

DO NOT create dramatic breath fog - it looks unnatural!


DANGEROUS PHRASES (Avoid for cold scenes):
AVOID THESE:
- "breath visible in cold"
- "breath puffs out"
- "breath fog"
- "breathing visible"
- "steam from mouth"
- "exhale visible"

These trigger dramatic smoke effects!
USE INSTEAD (to show cold):
- "snow flakes catching on his hood"
- "frost visible on his stubble"
- "cheeks reddened from cold"
- "shoulders hunched against wind"
- "snow accumulating on jacket"

"warm glow from fire" → Creates magical orange light everywhere
"small campfire in corner, contained light"

"some dust particles visible in sunbeam only"

DO NOT add dramatic atmospheric effects!

SHOT DURATION & PACING (CRITICAL!)
GROK LIMITATION: Grok generates minimum 6 seconds - this CANNOT be changed
through prompts.
WHY WE CAN’T USE “ACTION COMPLETE EARLY” HACK:
HACK BREAKS LASTFRAME WORKFLOW:

If action completes in 2 seconds → Character freezes
Remaining 4 seconds → Frozen/dead frames
Last frame → Awkward frozen pose
Next clip → Starts from weird frame = DISASTER!

Our workflow depends on LASTFRAME for continuity.
Frozen awkward lastframe = broken chain!


ACTUAL SOLUTION: Plan shots that FILL 6 seconds meaningfully!
Since every clip WILL be 6 seconds, plan content that FILLS 6 seconds:
CORRECT APPROACH:

Instead of: "Feet close-up" (2 sec content stretched to 6)
Plan: "Feet walking through snow, 3-4 steps, crunching" (fills 6 sec)

Instead of: "Character looks at other" (2 sec of just staring)
Plan: "Character notices, processes, expression changes, then looks" (fills 6
sec)

Instead of: "Quick reaction shot" (2 sec reaction)
Plan: "Reaction builds - subtle first, grows, emotion develops" (fills 6 sec)

 step detail
Reaction Just staring Notice → Process → React → Emotion deepens →
 Hold
Look at Quick glance held Sense something → Turn slowly → Find person →
person forever Expression shifts
Detail shot Object sitting static Camera slowly reveals, light plays, dust particles
Establishing Static wide Slow push in + movement in scene (birds, wind,
 people)
Dialogue Just talking head Gestures, micro-expressions, breathing, natural
 movement

FAST PACING (Action scenes):

 - Post-edit: Trim clips shorter if needed

SLOW PACING (Emotional scenes):
 - FEWER shots
 - LESS action, more atmosphere
 - SLOWER camera movement

CAMERA REVEAL RULE (CRITICAL!)
THE PROBLEM: Camera movement that “reveals” new elements NOT in the reference
image causes those elements to MAGICALLY APPEAR!
step_3_0g.example_of_the_problem:
EXAMPLE OF THE PROBLEM:

Attached image: Lane with chai stall (shops NOT visible on right)
Prompt: "Camera pans right to reveal shuttered shops"

What happens:
 - Frame 1: Lane and chai stall (matching reference)
 - Frame 2: Camera pans right...
 - Frame 3: Shops SUDDENLY APPEAR! 
 - Frame 4: Full shops visible (spawned from nothing!)

Looks MAGICAL and UNNATURAL - shops materialized!


THE RULE:
CAMERA CANNOT "REVEAL" WHAT ISN'T IN THE REFERENCE!

If element is NOT visible in attached image →
Camera movement CANNOT bring it "into view" →
Because Grok will SPAWN it from nowhere!

Camera can only:
 - Move TOWARD elements already visible
 - Get CLOSER to elements already in frame
 - Move WITHIN the visible scene area
 - NOT pan/tilt to areas not shown in reference

step_3_0g.problem_1_camera_speed_inconsistency:
PROBLEM 1: CAMERA SPEED INCONSISTENCY
THE ISSUE:
Clip 1: Dolly in at SLOW speed
Clip 2: Dolly in continues but FASTER
Clip 3: Dolly in continues but SLOWER

step_3_0g.solution_explicit_speed_specification:
SOLUTION: Explicit Speed Specification
Define speed with MEASURABLE terms:
SPEED DEFINITIONS:
 - VERY SLOW: Almost imperceptible movement (1-2 inches per second)
 - SLOW: Gentle, deliberate movement (3-5 inches per second)
 - MEDIUM: Normal walking pace movement
 - FAST: Quick, urgent movement
 - VERY FAST: Rapid, action-sequence movement

Camera Speed Lock Template:
CAMERA SPEED LOCK:

Movement Type: DOLLY IN (forward toward subject)
Speed: VERY SLOW - approximately 2-3 inches per second
Consistency: This EXACT speed must match previous clip
Reference: Camera was moving at this speed in attached image

SPECIFIC MEASUREMENT:
- In 6 seconds, camera moves forward approximately 12-18 inches
- Movement is BARELY PERCEPTIBLE but continuous
- DO NOT speed up or slow down from previous clip
- Maintain IDENTICAL pace throughout

Speed comparison:
- NOT as slow as completely static
- NOT as fast as walking pace
- EXACTLY matching the gentle drift of previous clip

Speed Description Phrases:

Speed Level Use These Phrases
Very Slow “barely perceptible drift,” “glacial pace,” “almost static”
Slow “gentle movement,” “deliberate drift,” “leisurely pace”
Medium “steady movement,” “walking pace,” “moderate speed”
Fast “quick movement,” “urgent pace,” “rapid motion”

Example - Continuous Dolly:
CLIP 2.1:
"Camera begins VERY SLOW dolly in toward the desk.
Speed: Glacial pace, barely perceptible forward drift.
In 6 seconds, camera moves approximately 12-15 inches closer."

CLIP 2.2:
" CAMERA SPEED CONTINUITY:
Continue the EXACT same dolly in motion from previous clip.
Speed: VERY SLOW - IDENTICAL to previous clip's pace.
The movement should feel like ONE continuous shot.
In 6 seconds, camera continues forward another 12-15 inches.
DO NOT change speed - maintain the glacial drift."

CLIP 2.3:
" CAMERA SPEED CONTINUITY:
SAME dolly in, SAME speed as previous two clips.
Speed: VERY SLOW - matching exactly.
This should feel like minute 0:12-0:18 of one long take.
NO acceleration, NO deceleration."

Color Drift Prevention Template:

step_3_0e.step_30e_storytelling_in_every:
Step 3.0E: STORYTELLING IN EVERY PROMPT (CRITICAL!)


AUDIO SYSTEM - Complete Guide
Audio has FOUR components that must be handled separately:
 1. NARRATION - Voice-over storytelling
 2. DIALOGUE - Character speech
 3. BACKGROUND MUSIC - Mood/atmosphere music
 4. SOUND EFFECTS - Environmental/action sounds


1 ⃣ NARRATION FORMAT
NARRATION QUALITY - MOST CRITICAL SECTION! 
GENERIC POETRY ≠ GOOD NARRATION
"Kuch raaz safar maangte hain..." = GARBAGE!
This is the #1 mistake AI makes!
DO NOT write vague philosophical poetry!


THE NARRATION DISEASE - “POETRY SYNDROME”
SYMPTOMS OF BAD NARRATION (Poetry Syndrome):

1. EVERY line has "..." dramatic pause
2. EVERY sentence sounds philosophical
3. ZERO specific details (names, places, dates)
4. ZERO story information
5. Sounds like shayari, not storytelling
6. Audience learns NOTHING new
step_3_0e.example_of_the_disease:
EXAMPLE OF THE DISEASE:
"Faisalabad ki in purani galiyon mein...
kuch jagahen aisi hoti hain...
jo sirf ghar nahi hotin... yaad hoti hain.
Aur kuch yaadein... insaan se sirf waqt nahi...
himmat bhi maangti hain."

WHAT'S WRONG:
 - "kuch jagahen" = WHICH places? NAME them!
 - "yaad hoti hain" = WHOSE memory? WHAT happened?
 - "himmat maangti hain" = Generic philosophy!
 - Every line = "..." = Overdramatic!
 - Audience learns = ABSOLUTELY NOTHING!
 - This is LAZY WRITING disguised as depth!


NARRATION QUALITY TEST - 5 QUESTIONS
Before finalizing ANY narration, ask these 5 questions:
QUESTION 1: Does it have SPECIFIC NAMES?
"ek shakhs" → + "Professor Danish Mirza"
"purani gali" → + "Aminpur Bazaar ki Haveli #47"
"ek kitaab" → + "1847 ki handwritten diary"
QUESTION 2: Does it have SPECIFIC NUMBERS?
"kaafi saal pehle" → + "35 saal pehle, 1989 mein"
"door tak" → + "487 kilometer door, Kashmir"
"kuch log" → + "sirf 3 log jaante the"
QUESTION 3: Does it CREATE A QUESTION in audience mind?
"raaz tha" → + "raaz jo 3 logon ki jaan le chuka tha"
(Audience thinks: "KAUN mare? KYUN? KYA raaz tha?")
QUESTION 4: Does it have STAKES (consequences)?
"mushkil tha" → + "fail hue to wapis nahi aa sakte"
"khatarnak" → + "pichle 3 jo gaye woh laute nahi"
QUESTION 5: Is it FREE of excessive "..." pauses?
"Kuch raaz... safar maangte... aur kuch..."
"35 saal pehle Danish Sahab yahan se nikle the.
Unke haath mein ek naqsha tha. Woh laute nahi."

If ANY answer is NO → REWRITE the narration!


vs + FULL NARRATION COMPARISON
SAME STORY - Two Ways:
GARBAGE NARRATION (Poetry Syndrome):

"Faisalabad ki in purani galiyon mein...
kuch jagahen aisi hoti hain... jo sirf ghar nahi hotin...
yaad hoti hain.

Aur kuch yaadein... insaan se sirf waqt nahi...
himmat bhi maangti hain.

Is kahani ka raasta... ek kitaab se khulta hai.
Aur ek qasam se.

Do dost... ek hi bike... aur ek aisa cipher...
jo seedha Kashmir tak le jaata hai.

Lekin... jab raaz ki talash shuru hoti hai...
raaz bhi talash shuru kar deta hai."
step_3_0e.problems:
PROBLEMS:
 - "kuch jagahen" = WHICH? No name!
 - "yaadein himmat maangti" = Generic philosophy!
 - "ek kitaab" = WHICH book? What's in it?
 - "ek qasam" = WHAT promise? To whom?
 - "cipher" = What cipher? Where from?
 - "raaz talash karta hai" = Meaningless poetry!
 - EVERY line has "..." = Overdramatic!
 - Information given = ZERO!

ENGAGING NARRATION (Proper Storytelling):

"Faisalabad ke Aminpur Bazaar mein ek haveli hai,
number 47. Log ise 'Kitaabon Wala Ghar' kehte hain.

35 saal pehle, 1989 ki ek raat, yahan se Professor
Danish Mirza ghayab ho gaye. Unke haath mein ek
naqsha tha - 1847 ki Dogra War ka - jo seedha
Kashmir ke un pahadon tak le jaata hai jahan
aaj bhi koi nahi jaata.

Danish Sahab ke pote, Zain ne jab dada ki purani
diary kholi, usne dekha ek cipher - Dogra code -
jo 150 saal se koi crack nahi kar paaya tha.

Diary ke aakhri page pe likha tha:
'Jo yeh raaz dhundne jayega... woh akela nahi jayega.
Raaz bhi uske saath chalega.'

Aur Zain ne faisla kar liya - apne dost Hamza ke
saath, ek purani bike pe, 487 kilometer ka safar.
Faisalabad se Kashmir. Jawab dhundne."

WHAT'S BETTER:
 - "Haveli #47, Aminpur Bazaar" = SPECIFIC!
 - "35 saal pehle, 1989" = SPECIFIC time!
 - "Professor Danish Mirza" = SPECIFIC name!
 - "1847 Dogra War naqsha" = SPECIFIC object!
 - "Pote Zain, dost Hamza" = SPECIFIC characters!
 - "487 kilometer" = SPECIFIC distance!
 - "Dogra code, 150 saal" = SPECIFIC mystery!
 - "Diary quote" = SPECIFIC hook!
 - Audience CURIOSITY = HIGH!
 - Story SETUP = COMPLETE!
BANNED PHRASES - NEVER USE!
BANNED - NEVER WRITE THESE:
• "Kuch raaz... safar maangte hain"
• "Kuch kahaniyan... sunai nahi jaatin"
• "Waqt ke saath... kuch cheezein badal jaati hain"
• "Har jagah ki... apni kahani hoti hai"
• "Kuch yaadein... waqt nahi mitaa sakta"
• "In purani galiyon mein... waqt thehar gaya"
• "Zindagi mein... kuch mod aise aate hain"
• "Manzil se zyada... safar zaroori hai"
These are LAZY, GENERIC, MEANINGLESS!


OPENING NARRATION TEMPLATES
Template 1: Location + Event + Mystery
"[Specific Place] mein ek [building] hai.
[X] saal pehle yahan [event] hua tha.
[Name] ke saath [thing] tha - jo aaj tak [mystery]."

Template 2: Character + Discovery + Stakes
"[Name] ko nahi pata tha ki [object] mein [thing] milegi.
Ek aisi [desc] jo [X years] pehle [person] ne chhupai thi.
Aur jo dhundne gaye... [stakes]."


CLIP-WISE NARRATION FLOW


CRITICAL: Narration is NOT per clip - JUST LIKE BG MUSIC!
NARRATION = ONE continuous audio across MULTIPLE clips
Same as BG Music:
• BG Music: 3-6 clips = ONE track
• Narration: 3-5 clips = ONE continuous voiceover
NOT separate narration for each 6-second clip!
WRONG (Per-clip narration - CHOPPY & UNNATURAL!):

Clip 1.1 Narration: "Faisalabad ki galiyon mein..."
Clip 1.2 Narration: "Kuch jagahen yaad hoti hain..."
Clip 1.3 Narration: "Is kahani ka raasta..."
Clip 1.4 Narration: "Do dost, ek bike..."
step_3_0e.part_4:
PROBLEMS:
 - Sounds like SEPARATE voiceovers glued together
 - No natural FLOW
 - Audience notices the CUTS
 - Real movies NEVER do this!
 - This is NOT how professional narration works!


CORRECT (Multi-clip continuous - LIKE BG MUSIC!):

NARRATION BLOCK - Clips 1.1 to 1.4

CLIPS COVERED: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4

number 47. 35 saal pehle, 1989 ki ek raat,
Professor Danish Mirza ghayab ho gaye. Unke haath
mein ek naqsha tha - 1847 ki Dogra War ka - jo
seedha Kashmir ke un pahadon tak le jaata hai

NARRATION COVERAGE GUIDE:

 - Clips 7-8: Closing narration (12 sec)

NEVER: Separate narration for each clip!


SILENCE IS POWERFUL!
60-70% clips: SILENT or dialogue only
30-40% clips: Narration

NOT every scene needs narration!
NOT every clip within narration scenes needs voiceover!

USE NARRATION FOR:

STAY SILENT FOR:

2 ⃣ DIALOGUE FORMAT


DIALOGUE QUALITY - CRITICAL RULES! 
GENERIC FILMY LINES ≠ GOOD DIALOGUE
"Copy." "Samajh gaya." "Roger that." = GARBAGE!
Real people DON'T talk like military movies!
THE DIALOGUE DISEASE - “FILMY SYNDROME”
SYMPTOMS OF BAD DIALOGUE:

1. Generic military/spy clichés ("Copy", "Roger", "Target acquired")
2. Fake deep philosophy ("Ilm amanat hai", "Waqt sabka aata hai")
3. Information dumps disguised as conversation
4. Every character sounds THE SAME
5. No natural pauses, hesitations, or incomplete sentences
6. Sounds like BAD DUBBING, not real talk
step_3_0e.part_5:
EXAMPLE OF THE DISEASE:
"Plan?"
"Simple nahi. Seedha zaroor."
"Copy."
"Samajh gaya."
"Ready?"
"Ilm amanat hai. Ready rehna parta hai."

WHAT'S WRONG:
 - "Copy" "Samajh gaya" = Military movie clichés!
 - "Ilm amanat hai" = Fake philosophy (cringe!)
 - "Simple nahi. Seedha zaroor" = Trying too hard to sound cool
 - Both characters sound IDENTICAL
 - Real friends NEVER talk like this!
 - This is LAZY WRITING!


DIALOGUE QUALITY TEST - 5 QUESTIONS
Before finalizing ANY dialogue, ask:
Q1: Would a REAL person say this in real life?
"Ilm amanat hai" → + "Yaar, serious hai yeh"
"Copy" → + "Theek" or just a NOD (no words!)
Q2: Does each character have a UNIQUE voice?
Both say formal lines → + Zain serious, Hamza casual
Zain: "Dekh, seedha point pe aata hoon"
Hamza: "Haan bhai, bol na"
Q3: Is it FREE of military/spy clichés?
"Roger", "Copy", "Target confirmed", "Mission accomplished"
"Theek hai", "Hmm", "Chal", "Samjha"
Q4: Is it FREE of fake philosophy?
"Waqt sabka aata hai", "Manzil door nahi"
Just say what you mean, directly!
Q5: Can some lines be SILENT instead?
"Samajh gaya" (words) → + Just a nod (visual)
"Ready?" "Haan" → + Eye contact + nod (no words)

If ANY answer is NO → REWRITE the dialogue!


vs + DIALOGUE COMPARISON
GARBAGE DIALOGUE (Filmy Syndrome):

HAMZA: "Plan?"
ZAIN: "Simple nahi. Seedha zaroor."
HAMZA: "Copy."

(later)
ZAIN: "Do choke points. Sitarah = route change. Chaand = hide."
HAMZA: "Samajh gaya."

(later)
HAMZA: "Ready?"
ZAIN: "Ilm amanat hai. Ready rehna parta hai."
step_3_0e.part_6:
PROBLEMS:
 - "Copy" = Who talks like this? Military movie!
 - "Samajh gaya" = Generic acknowledgment
 - "Simple nahi. Seedha zaroor" = Trying to sound cool
 - "Ilm amanat hai" = Fake deep (cringe!)
 - Both sound like ROBOTS, not friends
 - Zero personality difference!

NATURAL DIALOGUE (Real Conversation):

HAMZA: "Yaar, subah subah... kya scene hai?"
ZAIN: "Dekh, seedha point pe aata hoon. Professor ka khat mila."
HAMZA: "Kaun professor?"
ZAIN: "Raza Mehdi. Kashmir wala cipher... uska pata chal gaya."
HAMZA: (eyebrows up, leans in) "Serious?"
ZAIN: (nods) "Aaj nikalna hai. Islamabad via, phir Muzaffarabad."
HAMZA: (thinking, then) "Chal, theek hai. Kab nikalein?"
ZAIN: "Ek ghante mein."
(beat - both look at each other)
HAMZA: (small smile) "Meri bike chalegi?"
ZAIN: (slight smile back) "Teri hi chalani hai."

WHAT'S BETTER:
 - "Yaar, subah subah" = How real friends greet
 - "Kaun professor?" = Natural question
 - "Serious?" = Real reaction, not "Copy"
 - Character voices DIFFERENT (Hamza casual, Zain focused)
 - "Meri bike chalegi?" = Personality moment!
 - Some beats are SILENT (just looks, nods)
 - Sounds like REAL conversation!


BANNED DIALOGUE PHRASES - NEVER USE!
MILITARY/SPY CLICHÉS:
• "Copy" / "Roger" / "Affirmative"
• "Target confirmed" / "Mission accomplished"
• "Move out" / "Let's roll"
• "We have a situation"
• "Go dark" / "Radio silence"
FAKE PHILOSOPHY:
• "Ilm amanat hai"
• "Waqt sabka aata hai"
• "Manzil door nahi, raasta mushkil hai"
• "Zindagi mein kuch paane ke liye..."
• "Himmat aur hausla..."
GENERIC RESPONSES:
• "Samajh gaya" (use nod instead!)
• "Theek hai, samjha" (use "Hmm" or silence!)
• "Plan clear hai"
• "Ready?" "Ready." (use eye contact instead!)


CHARACTER VOICE DIFFERENTIATION
Each character MUST have a DISTINCT way of speaking:
step_3_0e.example_two_friends:

THEY SHOULD NOT SOUND THE SAME!


SILENT BEATS - USE THEM!
NOT every moment needs dialogue!

NOT: 100% dialogue in every clip!

step_3_0e.7_narration_vs_silence_guide:
### 7⃣ NARRATION vs SILENCE GUIDE

**Not every clip needs narration! Strategic silence is powerful.**

WHEN TO USE NARRATION:  Scene openings (set the mood)  Time jumps (“Do
saal baad…”)  Inner thoughts (what character feels)  Mystery building (hint at
secrets)  Emotional context (why this matters)  Story bridges (connecting scenes)
WHEN TO USE SILENCE (No narration):  Action moments (let visuals speak) 
Dialogue scenes (characters talking)  Discovery/reveal moments (audience needs to
absorb)  Tension peaks (silence builds suspense)  Emotional climaxes (music +
visuals only)  Visual beauty shots (let audience appreciate)  After important
dialogue (let it land)
RATIO GUIDE:  60-70% of clips: SILENT or dialogue only  30-40% of clips:
Narration  NOT every clip needs voiceover!

---

**THE PROBLEM:**
Technical prompts become SOULLESS - all camera movements, locks, and specs
but NO STORY!

CURRENT ISSUE:

Prompt has:  Camera position   Visual continuity   Object lock  
Technical specs   NARRATION? - MISSING! STORY HOOK? - MISSING! EMOTION?
MISSING!
Result: Technically perfect but BORING video! Audience: “Kya dekh raha hoon? Kyun dekh
raha hoon?”

---

**SOLUTION: Every Clip Must Have STORY PURPOSE!**

**Three Questions for EVERY clip:**

Before writing any prompt, answer:
1⃣ WHAT is happening? (Action/Event) 2⃣ WHY does audience care? (Emotional hook) 3⃣
WHAT are they hearing? (Narration/Dialogue)
If you can’t answer all three → Clip needs work!
