narration_rules.cinematic_pacing_system_hollywoodstandar:
##  CINEMATIC PACING SYSTEM (Hollywood-Standard)

     BLOCKBUSTER PACING RULES - STRICTLY FOLLOW!   
Based on: Mission Impossible, Uncharted, Jumanji,   San Andreas, Jungle Cruise, The
Mummy, Titanic     Different scene types = Different pacing = Different   camera
work = Different clip structure!  

---

###  SCENE TYPE IDENTIFICATION (Do This FIRST!)

Before writing ANY scene, identify its TYPE:

SCENE TYPES:  TYPE A: ACTION/CHASE (Running, fighting, escaping)  TYPE B:
SUSPENSE/THRILLER (Building tension, reveals)  TYPE C: EXPLORATION/DISCOVERY
(Finding clues, solving puzzles)  TYPE D: CONVERSATION/DIALOGUE (Two or more
people talking)  TYPE E: EMOTIONAL/INTIMATE (Romance, grief, bonding) 
TYPE F: DESTRUCTION/DISASTER (Large scale chaos)  TYPE G:
OPENING/ESTABLISHING (Scene introduction)  TYPE H: TRANSITION/BREATHING
(Recovery between intensity)

---
narration_rules.type_a_actionchase_sequences:
## TYPE A: ACTION/CHASE SEQUENCES  

  HOLLYWOOD RULE: Action = RAPID visual changes within shots   
Real movies: 0.5-1.5 second cuts   Your workflow: 6-second clips with MAXIMUM
internal action

### ACTION SCENE STRUCTURE (Per 6-second clip):

PATTERN: ACTION → REACTION → ACTION → RESULT
Within EACH 6-second clip, include:  Seconds 0-2: Action begins
(running/fighting/escaping)  Seconds 2-3: Face reaction (fear/determination/effort)
 - Seconds 3-5: Action continues/escalates  Seconds 5-6: Result/setup for next clip
CAMERA MUST BE DYNAMIC:  Push-in toward action  Follow movement
(tracking)  Slight shake for intensity (describe as “handheld feel”)  NEVER static
during action!

### ACTION CLIP CYCLING (4-clip pattern):

CLIP 1 (Wide):  Show full action scale  Character small in frame, environment big
 - Establishes WHAT is happening and WHERE  Camera: Wide tracking or slight
push-in
CLIP 2 (Medium):  Focus on character movement  Upper body visible,
running/fighting  Details of action visible  Camera: Following character
CLIP 3 (Close):  Face showing emotion/effort  Hands doing action (gripping,
reaching)  Maximum emotional connection  Camera: Tight on face/hands
CLIP 4 (Wide/Result):  Show outcome of action sequence  New obstacle OR
escape achieved  Setup for next action beat  Camera: Pull back to reveal
THEN REPEAT CYCLE with escalating intensity!


### ACTION SCENE - LASTFRAME HANDLING:

  CRITICAL: Action clips CANNOT use simple lastframe!     Problem:
Character position changes DRAMATICALLY between   frames during action. Lastframe
shows position X, but next   clip needs to start from position Y.
SOLUTION - ACTION SCENE LASTFRAME RULES:
OPTION 1: NEW IMAGE for each action clip (SAFEST)  Generate fresh image for each
clip  Describe exact starting position  No continuity errors  Best for: Running,
chasing, major movement
OPTION 2: LASTFRAME only if end position = start position  Character ends clip in
HOLDABLE position  Example: Running → reaches wall → STOPS → next clip continues
from wall  The “STOP POINT” is your lastframe  Best for: Pause moments, catches
breath, looks around
OPTION 3: LASTFRAME with POSITION OVERRIDE  Use lastframe for ENVIRONMENT
consistency only  Describe character in NEW POSITION in prompt  “The attached
image shows the cave (use for environment). The character has now moved to the LEFT
side of frame…”  Best for: Maintaining location look while moving character
 ACTION SEQUENCE EXAMPLE (Chase through cave):
CLIP 3.1 (Wide - NEW IMAGE):  Image: Character at cave entrance, about to run 
Video: Runs 8 feet into cave  ENDS WITH: Character mid-stride, deeper in cave
CLIP 3.2 (Medium - NEW IMAGE, not lastframe!):  WHY: Character position changed
too much  Image: Character now 15 feet inside cave, still running  Video:
Continues running, looks back over shoulder  ENDS WITH: Character reaching narrow
passage
CLIP 3.3 (Close - LASTFRAME OK here):  WHY: Previous clip ended with character at
specific spot  Lastframe: Character at narrow passage  Video: Close on face, fear +
determination, squeezes through  ENDS WITH: Face emerging on other side
CLIP 3.4 (Wide - NEW IMAGE):  WHY: New environment (other side of passage) 
Image: New cave chamber, character entering from left  Video: Stops, looks around,
sees something  ENDS WITH: Character frozen, looking at discovery

---
narration_rules.type_b_suspensethriller_sequences:
## TYPE B: SUSPENSE/THRILLER SEQUENCES 

  HOLLYWOOD RULE: Suspense = SLOW BUILD then SUDDEN payoff  
Shot length DECREASES as tension INCREASES   Long shots (calm) → Medium →
Short → VERY SHORT (peak)

### SUSPENSE SCENE STRUCTURE:

THE SUSPENSE LADDER (7-clip pattern):
CLIP 1 - Establishing Calm (6s, minimal movement):  Wide shot, character in
environment  Slow camera, almost static  “Something feels off” atmosphere 
SOUND: Quiet, ambient
CLIP 2 - First Hint (6s, subtle movement):  Character notices something  Camera
slow push toward subject  Detail shot: shadow, sound source, object  SOUND:
Subtle hint
CLIP 3 - Investigation (6s, measured movement):  Character approaches cautiously
 - Camera follows at same pace  Tension building through slowness  SOUND:
Footsteps emphasized
CLIP 4 - False Scare (6s, sudden spike):  Something harmless revealed (rat, falling
object)  Quick movement, character startles  Relief moment  SOUND: Sharp
then quiet
CLIP 5 - Real Threat Setup (6s, building):  Character relaxes… but camera sees
something they don’t  Slow camera drift to reveal threat  Audience knows,
character doesn’t  SOUND: Low tension drone
CLIP 6 - Character Realizes (6s, accelerating):  Character turns, sees threat 
Maximum movement in reaction  Face close-up with fear  SOUND: Sharp sting
CLIP 7 - Payoff/Escape (6s, maximum intensity):  Full action response 
Running/fighting/hiding  Fast camera movement  SOUND: Full intensity


### SUSPENSE SCENE - LASTFRAME HANDLING:

SUSPENSE LASTFRAME RULES:
CLIPS 1-4 (Slow buildup): LASTFRAME works well  Minimal position change 
Environment consistency important  Character in same general area
CLIP 5 (Threat reveal): Consider NEW IMAGE  Camera angle may change to show
threat  New element (threat) entering frame  May need different composition
CLIPS 6-7 (Payoff): Treat as ACTION (see Type A rules)  Rapid position changes 
Often need NEW IMAGE  Or use “stop point” lastframe strategy

---
narration_rules.type_c_explorationdiscovery_sequences:
## TYPE C: EXPLORATION/DISCOVERY SEQUENCES 

  HOLLYWOOD RULE: Discovery = SHOW → REACT → EXAMINE → REVEAL
   Never just show the discovery - show the PROCESS   Character’s wonder =
Audience’s wonder

### DISCOVERY SCENE STRUCTURE:

THE DISCOVERY SEQUENCE (6-clip pattern):
CLIP 1 - Approach:  Character approaching location/object  Environment visible,
object in distance  Curiosity on face  Camera: Following or preceding character
CLIP 2 - First Look:  Character sees it clearly for first time  Reaction shot - awe,
confusion, recognition  Camera: Close on face, then what they see (POV)
CLIP 3 - Examination:  Character moves closer, touches/inspects  Details of object
visible  Hands interacting (carefully)  Camera: Medium on hands + object
CLIP 4 - Detail Discovery:  Close-up on specific important detail  The CLUE or KEY
element  Character’s finger points or traces  Camera: Extreme close
CLIP 5 - Realization:  Character’s face - “eureka” moment  Putting pieces together
 - Eyes widen, nod, or verbal reaction  Camera: Close on face
CLIP 6 - Context/Result:  Pull back to show character + discovery  New
understanding established  Setup for next action  Camera: Medium-wide


### EXPLORATION - LASTFRAME HANDLING:

EXPLORATION LASTFRAME RULES:
MOSTLY USE LASTFRAME - Movement is controlled!  Character moves deliberately,
not frantically  Environment stays consistent  Position changes are small and
predictable
EXCEPTION - Shot type changes:  Wide → Close: NEW IMAGE (different framing) 
Close → Wide: NEW IMAGE (different framing)  Same shot type continues:
LASTFRAME OK
EXAMPLE:  Clip 1 (Wide): Character enters room → LASTFRAME OK for Clip 2 if also
wide  Clip 2 (Medium): Approaches desk → NEW IMAGE needed  Clip 3 (Close):
Examines object → NEW IMAGE needed (different shot type)  Clip 4 (Extreme Close):
Detail → NEW IMAGE needed (different shot type)  Clip 5 (Close): Face reaction →
NEW IMAGE needed (back to face)  Clip 6 (Wide): Context → NEW IMAGE needed
(different shot type)

---
narration_rules.type_d_conversationdialogue_sequences:
## TYPE D: CONVERSATION/DIALOGUE SEQUENCES 

  HOLLYWOOD RULE: Dialogue = Longer shots, stable camera     Let
words land. Don’t distract with movement.   Cut on dialogue beats, not arbitrary timing.

### DIALOGUE SCENE STRUCTURE:

THE CONVERSATION PATTERN:
CLIP 1 - Establishing Two-Shot:  Both characters in frame  Shows spatial
relationship  Environment context  Minimal camera movement (subtle push-in
OK)
CLIP 2 - Speaker A (Over-shoulder B):  Focus on person speaking  Other person’s
shoulder/back in foreground  Listener partly visible  Camera: Static or very slow
push
CLIP 3 - Speaker B (Over-shoulder A):  Reverse of previous  Focus on responding
person  First speaker’s shoulder in foreground  Camera: Static or very slow push
CLIP 4 - Reaction/Close-up:  Key emotional reaction  Single face, no over-shoulder
 - Held longer for impact  Camera: Static, intimate
CLIP 5 - Two-Shot Resolution:  Back to both characters  Conversation concludes
or shifts  Prepares for transition  Camera: May pull back slightly
REPEAT 2-3-4 as needed for longer conversations


### DIALOGUE - LASTFRAME HANDLING:

DIALOGUE LASTFRAME RULES:
CRITICAL ISSUE: Characters are STATIONARY  Lastframe shows same position 
Works well for continuity  BUT shot type changes need NEW IMAGE
OVER-SHOULDER SWITCHES - ALWAYS NEW IMAGE:  Over-shoulder A → Over-
shoulder B = NEW IMAGE  These are OPPOSITE camera positions!  Cannot use
lastframe for reverse angles
SAME ANGLE CONTINUES - LASTFRAME OK:  Over-shoulder A continues →
LASTFRAME OK  Person keeps talking in same framing  Works for multi-line
speeches
TWO-SHOT - LASTFRAME USUALLY OK:  Both characters visible throughout 
Position relatively stable  Good for reaction moments

---
narration_rules.type_e_emotionalintimate_sequences:
## TYPE E: EMOTIONAL/INTIMATE SEQUENCES  

  HOLLYWOOD RULE: Emotion = SLOW, HELD shots     Titanic-style:
5-8 second average shot length   Let emotions BREATHE. Silence is powerful.

### EMOTIONAL SCENE STRUCTURE:
THE EMOTIONAL MOMENT PATTERN:
CLIP 1 - Context:  Wide or medium, character in environment  Slow, dreamlike
camera movement  Establishes mood  MINIMAL action - stillness is key
CLIP 2 - Approach/Connection:  Two characters coming together  OR single
character approaching meaningful object  Slow, deliberate movement  Camera:
Gentle tracking or static
CLIP 3 - Intimate Close:  Face close-up - full emotion  Held LONGER than
comfortable  Eyes, small expressions  Camera: Static or imperceptible push
CLIP 4 - The Moment:  The key emotional beat  Touch, look, realization 
Minimum movement, maximum feeling  Camera: May be static entirely
CLIP 5 - Aftermath:  Reaction to moment  Processing emotion  Slight
movement (breath, blink)  Camera: Holds
CLIP 6 - Context Return:  Pull back to wider shot  Shows characters in
environment  Peaceful, resolved  Camera: Slow pull-back or crane up


### EMOTIONAL - LASTFRAME HANDLING:

EMOTIONAL SCENE LASTFRAME RULES:
ALMOST ALWAYS LASTFRAME WORKS:  Minimal movement throughout  Same
characters, same positions  Consistency creates intimacy
ONLY NEW IMAGE FOR:  Major shot type change (wide → extreme close)  New
character enters  Time passage within scene
SPECIAL NOTE - STILLNESS:  For emotional scenes, describe STILLNESS 
“Character remains in same position, only breathing visible”  “Eyes fixed on
[object/person], body still”  Movement should be MICRO (blink, breath, slight head
turn)

---
narration_rules.type_f_destructiondisaster_sequences:
## TYPE F: DESTRUCTION/DISASTER SEQUENCES 

  HOLLYWOOD RULE: Chaos = SCALE + DETAIL cycling rapidly   
Show enormity (wide) then human stakes (close) then   enormity again. Keep cycling.

### DESTRUCTION SCENE STRUCTURE:
THE DESTRUCTION CYCLE (5-clip repeating pattern):
CLIP 1 - Wide Scale:  Full destruction visible  Buildings falling, explosions, water
rushing  Characters SMALL in frame  Camera: Wide, may be shaking slightly
CLIP 2 - Medium Running:  Characters fleeing  Running toward/away from
camera  Destruction visible behind them  Camera: Tracking with characters
CLIP 3 - Close Emotion:  Face showing fear, determination  Quick beat of human
connection  Audience reminder of stakes  Camera: Tight on face
CLIP 4 - Insert Destruction:  Specific destruction detail  Falling debris, cracking
ground, fire spreading  No people, just chaos  Camera: Close on destruction
CLIP 5 - Wide Result:  New state of destruction  Characters in new position 
Setup for next cycle  Camera: Wide establishing
REPEAT with ESCALATING destruction!


### DESTRUCTION - LASTFRAME HANDLING:

DESTRUCTION LASTFRAME RULES:
ALMOST NEVER USE LASTFRAME:  Everything changes constantly  Environment
transforms  Character positions change dramatically
NEW IMAGE FOR EVERY CLIP (Recommended):  Describe current state of destruction
 - Character in new position  Environment has changed since last clip
IF MUST USE LASTFRAME:  Only for CLOSE shots on character  When character is
momentarily stationary  Background should be out-of-focus (hides changes)
DESTRUCTION CONTINUITY:  Track destruction STATE across clips  “Building
was intact → cracked → partially collapsed → rubble”  Each clip shows NEXT stage of
destruction

---
narration_rules.type_g_openingestablishing_sequences:
## TYPE G: OPENING/ESTABLISHING SEQUENCES 

  HOLLYWOOD RULE: Opening = Set the world, mood, stakes   
Wide, slow, atmospheric. Let audience ABSORB.   No rush. First impression matters
most.

### OPENING SCENE STRUCTURE:
THE OPENING SEQUENCE (5-clip pattern):
CLIP 1 - Extreme Wide/Drone:  Massive scale - landscape, city, era  No characters
OR tiny distant figures  Pure atmosphere and world  Camera: Slow drone/crane,
sweeping
CLIP 2 - Closer Wide:  More detail of location  Specific area/building in focus 
Maybe hint of activity  Camera: Slow push-in or tracking
CLIP 3 - Medium Context:  Entrance to main location  OR approach to main
character  Environment details clear  Camera: Deliberate, measured movement
CLIP 4 - Character Introduction:  Main character first appearance  Don’t show face
immediately (mystery)  Hands, back, silhouette first  Camera: Following or
revealing
CLIP 5 - Character Reveal:  Face visible for first time  Expression sets tone 
Held for recognition  Camera: Close or medium-close


### OPENING - LASTFRAME HANDLING:

OPENING SEQUENCE LASTFRAME RULES:
CLIPS 1-2: NEW IMAGE (Different scales)  Extreme wide → Wide requires new
composition  Drone shot → Ground shot requires new image
CLIPS 2-3: CONSIDER LASTFRAME  If continuous push-in toward location  Similar
framing continuing
CLIPS 3-4-5: MOSTLY NEW IMAGE  Different subjects (location → character) 
Different framings  Character reveal needs specific composition
GENERAL RULE FOR OPENINGS:  80% NEW IMAGE  20% LASTFRAME (only for
continuous camera moves)

---
narration_rules.type_h_transitionbreathing_sequences:
## TYPE H: TRANSITION/BREATHING SEQUENCES 

  HOLLYWOOD RULE: Breathing room = RECOVERY for audience   
After intensity, let them rest. Process what happened.   Slower pace, minimal action,
emotional landing.

### BREATHING ROOM STRUCTURE:
AFTER INTENSE SEQUENCE, INSERT 1-2 CLIPS:
BREATHING CLIP OPTION A - Environment:  Wide shot of location  No character
action  Just atmosphere, settling  Camera: Static or very slow drift
BREATHING CLIP OPTION B - Character Processing:  Close on face  No dialogue
 - Just breathing, thinking  Camera: Static, intimate
BREATHING CLIP OPTION C - Detail Focus:  Meaningful object  Related to what
just happened  Symbolic or plot-relevant  Camera: Slow push or static
PLACEMENT RULE:  After 3-4 intense clips: Insert 1 breathing clip  After major
action sequence: Insert 2 breathing clips  After emotional peak: Insert 1-2 breathing
clips  Before new sequence: Breathing helps transition

---
narration_rules.master_scene_type_reference_table:
##  MASTER SCENE TYPE REFERENCE TABLE

  SCENE TYPE  MOVEMENT  LASTFRAME  NEW IMAGE
  ACTION/CHASE  Maximum  Rarely  80-90%   SUSPENSE
Slow→Fast  Buildup OK  50-60%   EXPLORATION  Measured  Same shot OK  60-
70%   DIALOGUE  Minimal  Same angle OK  Reverse=New   EMOTIONAL
Minimal  Usually OK  30-40%   DESTRUCTION  Maximum  Rarely  90%+ 
OPENING  Slow+Grand  Rarely  80%+   BREATHING  Minimal  Usually OK  40-
50%

---
narration_rules.the_universal_shot_cycle:
##  THE UNIVERSAL SHOT CYCLE

    WIDE → MEDIUM → CLOSE → WIDE (repeat)     This cycle
applies to ALL scene types!   Adjust SPEED of cycle based on scene type:   
ACTION: Cycle every 2-3 clips   NORMAL: Cycle every 4-5 clips   SLOW: Cycle every
6-8 clips  
THE CYCLE EXPLAINED:
WIDE (Establishing):  Shows WHERE characters are  Shows SCALE of
environment  Gives context and geography  Use for: Opening shots, after major
action, scene transitions
MEDIUM (Action):  Shows characters from waist up  Body language visible 
Action details visible  Use for: Most dialogue, character movement
CLOSE (Emotion):  Face fills significant frame area  Eyes, expressions clear 
Maximum emotional connection  Use for: Reactions, realizations, key dialogue
THEN BACK TO WIDE for new context/cycle

---
narration_rules.reaction_shots_nonnegotiable_rule:
##  REACTION SHOTS - NON-NEGOTIABLE RULE

    EVERY ACTION NEEDS A REACTION SHOT!   
Blockbusters spend 30-40% of screen time on FACES   reacting to events. Without
reactions, audience   doesn’t know how to FEEL about what happened.  
REACTION PLACEMENT:
BEFORE major action: Show anticipation  Character sees what’s coming  Fear,
determination, preparation  Audience shares their perspective
DURING action: Show effort/emotion  Split second expressions  Pain, struggle,
focus  Keeps human stakes visible
AFTER major action: Show result emotionally  Relief, shock, grief, triumph 
Processing what happened  Audience processes WITH character
EXAMPLE SEQUENCE:  Clip 1: Character sees danger approaching (ANTICIPATION)
 - Clip 2: Action happens (EVENT)  Clip 3: Character’s face during (EFFORT) 
Clip 4: Result of action (OUTCOME)  Clip 5: Character reacts to result (PROCESSING)

---
narration_rules.pacing_rhythm_rule:
##  PACING RHYTHM RULE

    INTENSITY CYCLE - NEVER BREAK THIS PATTERN!     BUILD
(4-5 clips) → PEAK (2-3 clips) → BREATHE (1-2)   BUILD (4-5 clips) → PEAK (2-3 clips)
→ BREATHE (1-2)     Each BUILD should be slightly more intense than last   Until
CLIMAX (maximum peak, longest breathe after)  
NEVER:  10+ clips of continuous high intensity (exhausting)  5+ clips of
continuous low intensity (boring)  Peak without buildup (feels unearned)  Peak
without breathe (no release, no impact)
ALWAYS:  Earn every peak with proper build  Release every peak with breathing
room  Vary intensity throughout video  Biggest breathe after biggest peak

---
narration_rules.direction_spatial_orientation_critical:
##  DIRECTION & SPATIAL ORIENTATION (CRITICAL!)

    #1 CAUSE OF “WRONG DIRECTION” IMAGES:     AI
doesn’t know your STORY INTENT!     You THINK: “Soldiers approaching cave” 
You WRITE: “Soldiers on path near cave”   AI GENERATES: Soldiers facing AWAY (could
be leaving!)     SOLUTION: Explicitly describe FACING + MOVING direction!  

### THE DIRECTION PROBLEM EXPLAINED:

YOUR STORY INTENT: “Dogra soldiers are approaching the cave to capture the scholars”
YOUR PROMPT (WRONG): “12 soldiers with torches on mountain path, 60 feet from cave”

WHAT AI SEES:  12 soldiers   Torches   Mountain path   60 feet
from cave   Direction? - NOT SPECIFIED!  AI GUESSES → 50% chance of wrong
direction!
RESULT: Soldiers look like they’re LEAVING, not APPROACHING!

### DIRECTION SPECIFICATION RULES:

FOR EVERY MOVING SUBJECT, SPECIFY ALL THREE:
 1. FACING DIRECTION:  “Soldiers FACING the cave mouth”  “Character
 FACING camera”  “Man FACING away from camera”  “Group FACING left
 side of frame”

 2. MOVEMENT DIRECTION:  “Marching TOWARD the cave entrance” 
 “Running AWAY FROM the explosion”  “Walking INTO the room” 
 “Approaching FROM the right side”
 3. ORIENTATION TO KEY POINT:  “Lead soldier CLOSEST to cave”  “Front of
 group NEAREST to camera”  “Character positioned BETWEEN camera and
 door”  “Line extending AWAY from the cave down mountain”


### CAMERA + SUBJECT = WHAT WE SEE:

    THINK: “From THIS camera position, what SIDE of the   subject is
visible?”  
SCENARIO: Camera inside cave, soldiers outside approaching
WRONG ASSUMPTION:  Camera inside looking out  Soldiers climbing toward cave
 - We see their FRONTS? NO!
REALITY CHECK:  If soldiers are BETWEEN camera and the mountain behind them
 - And they’re facing UP toward camera/cave  Then YES, we see their FRONTS 
BUT IF:  Soldiers are on a path that goes PAST the cave  They might be facing
SIDEWAYS  We’d see their PROFILES
OR IF:  Soldiers already PASSED the cave view  Now climbing higher  We’d
see their BACKS!
SOLUTION: Be EXPLICIT about ALL of this!


### - vs + DIRECTION EXAMPLES:

 - WRONG - Ambiguous Direction:
“Wide shot from inside cave looking out. 12 Dogra soldiers with torches on the mountain
path, approximately 60 feet from the cave entrance, in single-file formation.”
PROBLEMS:  Which way are soldiers FACING? Unknown!  Are they coming or
going? Unknown!  Which end of line is closest to cave? Unknown!  What side of
soldiers do we SEE? Unknown!  Result: AI generates random direction!
 + CORRECT - Explicit Direction:
“Wide shot from inside cave looking out through the cave mouth.
SUBJECTS - DIRECTION EXPLICIT: Exactly 12 Dogra soldiers with 12 torches are visible
OUTSIDE on the mountain path, approximately 60 feet from cave entrance.
FACING: Soldiers are FACING the cave mouth - their torch-lit FRONTS are oriented toward
the camera/cave. We can see the orange glow illuminating the FRONT of their bodies and
faces (silhouetted).
MOVEMENT: They are marching TOWARD the cave entrance, climbing UP the path that
leads directly into THIS cave.
FORMATION: Single-file line. The LEAD soldier (at HEAD of line) is CLOSEST to the cave
entrance - he is the nearest figure to camera. The line extends BEHIND him, going DOWN
and AWAY from the cave, with the last soldier being farthest from cave.
VISUAL RESULT: From camera’s POV inside cave, we see soldiers’ FRONTS approaching us.
Lead soldier largest, others progressively smaller as line recedes into distance.“
WHAT’S BETTER:  FACING explicitly stated (toward cave)  MOVEMENT explicitly
stated (toward cave, climbing up)  FORMATION orientation clear (lead closest, line
behind)  VISUAL RESULT described (what camera actually sees)  ZERO ambiguity
= correct direction every time!

### DIRECTION CHECKLIST (Use for EVERY prompt with moving subjects):

FACING: Which direction is subject’s FRONT pointing? “facing the cave” / “facing
camera” / “facing left”

MOVING: Which direction is subject traveling? “marching toward” / “running away from”
/ “walking into”

RELATIVE POSITION: Where is subject relative to key point? “closest to cave” / “between
camera and door” / “nearest the edge”

FORMATION (if group): Which end is front, which is back? “lead soldier closest” / “front
of group at right” / “line extends behind”

CAMERA SEES: From this camera angle, what side is visible? “fronts visible” / “backs to
camera” / “profile view”

### COMMON DIRECTION SCENARIOS:

SCENARIO 1: Soldiers approaching cave (threat coming)  Camera: Inside cave looking
out  Soldiers: FACING cave, FRONTS toward camera  Formation: Lead soldier
CLOSEST to cave entrance  Movement: Climbing UP path TOWARD cave  We see:
Their FRONTS, getting larger as they approach
SCENARIO 2: Character running away from danger  Camera: Behind the character 
Character: FACING AWAY from camera  Movement: Running TOWARD
foreground/distance  We see: Their BACK, getting smaller
SCENARIO 3: Two characters facing each other  Camera: From the side  Character
A: FACING RIGHT (toward Character B)  Character B: FACING LEFT (toward Character
A)  We see: PROFILES of both
SCENARIO 4: Character entering room  Camera: Inside room  Character: At
doorway, FACING INTO room (toward camera)  Movement: Stepping FORWARD into
room  We see: Their FRONT as they enter
SCENARIO 5: Chase sequence (pursuer behind target)  Camera: Looking at both 
Target: In foreground, FACING AWAY, running  Pursuer: Behind target, FACING same
direction, chasing  We see: BACKS of both, pursuer closing distance

### DIRECTION WORDS REFERENCE:

TOWARD words: approaching, coming, advancing, heading to, marching to AWAY words:
leaving, retreating, fleeing, receding, departing FACING words: oriented toward, fronts
visible, looking at, turned to BACK words: backs to camera, facing away, turned from
FORMATION words:  “Lead/front at [location]”  “Line extends from X to Y” 
“Nearest to / Farthest from”  “Head of formation at”  “Tail of formation at”

narration_rules.scene_transitions_maintaining_momentum:
##  SCENE TRANSITIONS - MAINTAINING MOMENTUM

    BAD TRANSITIONS = Viewer loses interest between scenes 
GOOD TRANSITIONS = Viewer pulled INTO next scene     The moment between
scenes is CRITICAL!  

### THE TRANSITION PROBLEM:

BAD TRANSITION (Momentum Dies):
SCENE 1 ENDS: “Ibraheem ne kitaab chhupa di.” (Loop CLOSED. Story feels complete.)
SCENE 2 STARTS: “166 saal baad, Faisalabad mein ek ladka rehta tha…” (New topic. No
connection. Feels disconnected.)
PROBLEM:  Scene 1 loop fully closed = No reason to continue  Scene 2 starts fresh
= Feels like different video  No PULL into next scene  Energy DROPS between
scenes  Viewer might click away here!

### THE SOLUTION: BRIDGE TRANSITIONS

GOOD TRANSITION (Momentum Continues):
SCENE 1 ENDS: “Ibraheem ne kitaab chhupa di. Lekin marne se pehle, usne ek NISHANI
chhodi thi… apne khandaan ke liye.” (Loop partially closed + NEW LOOP opened!)
SCENE 2 STARTS: “166 saal baad. Faisalabad. Ibraheem ke parpoton ka parpota… Zain… usi
nishani ko dhundh raha tha.” (CONNECTS to Scene 1 loop!)
WHAT’S BETTER:  Scene 1 hints at what’s coming (nishani)  Scene 2 REFERENCES
Scene 1 mystery  Viewer wants to know: “Kya hai nishani?”  Smooth PULL from
past to present  Energy MAINTAINED between scenes  Viewer MUST continue
watching!

### TRANSITION TECHNIQUES:
TECHNIQUE 1: THE HOOK FORWARD
 End scene with hint about
NEXT scene:
“Ibraheem ne kitaab chhupa di. Lekin usne ek aur kaam kiya… jo 166 saal baad Zain ki
zindagi badal dega.”
→ Viewer thinks: “Kya kiya? Kaise badlega?” → MUST watch Scene 2!
TECHNIQUE 2: THE QUESTION BRIDGE
 End with question,
answer begins next scene:
Scene 1 ends: “Lekin sawaal yeh tha - kya raaz 166 saal baad bhi safe rahega?”
Scene 2 starts: “166 saal guzar gaye. Aur raaz safe tha… jab tak Zain ne woh diary nahi
kholi.”
→ Question from Scene 1 answered in Scene 2 → Smooth connection!
TECHNIQUE 3: THE VISUAL MATCH
 End and start on SIMILAR
visual:
Scene 1 ends: Close-up of OLD book being hidden (1858) Scene 2 starts: Close-up of SAME
book being found (Present)
OR
Scene 1 ends: Snow-covered mountains (Past) Scene 2 starts: Photo of same mountains on
wall (Present)
→ Visual LINK connects scenes!
TECHNIQUE 4: THE AUDIO BRIDGE
 Narration CONTINUES
over scene change:
“Ibraheem ne apni jaan de di… [VISUAL: Scene changes from 1858 to Present] …taake aaj
Zain is kamre mein khada ho sake.”
→ Voice creates continuity over visual cut!
TECHNIQUE 5: THE CONTRAST BRIDGE
 Deliberate contrast that
connects:
Scene 1 ends: “Us raat sirf ek CHEEKH suni gayi thi.” Scene 2 starts: “Aaj us haveli mein
KHAMOSHI hai.”
→ CHEEKH vs KHAMOSHI = contrast creates connection!
### SCENE TRANSITION CHECKLIST:

Does Scene end with FORWARD HOOK? (Hint about next)  Does Scene end with OPEN
LOOP? (Unanswered question)  Does next Scene REFERENCE previous scene?  Is there
VISUAL or AUDIO bridge?  Does energy MAINTAIN across transition?  Would viewer
feel PULL into next scene?
If ANY answer is NO → REWRITE TRANSITION!

### EXAMPLE: FULL TRANSITION MAPPING

 SCENE 1 → SCENE 2 TRANSITION:
 END SCENE 1: “Ibraheem ne kitaab chhupa di. Aur apne khoon se ek
NISHANI likhi… jo sirf uska khandaan samajh sake.” (FORWARD HOOK: What nishani?
What does it mean?)
START SCENE 2: “166 saal baad. Woh NISHANI ek purani diary mein mili - Zain ke haathon
mein.” (REFERENCES Scene 1 hook!)
 SCENE 2 → SCENE 3 TRANSITION:
 END SCENE 2: “Zain ne cipher solve kar liya. Answer ek location thi -
Kashmir mein. Lekin wahan jane ka matlab…” (OPEN LOOP: Kya matlab? Danger hint!)
START SCENE 3: “…487 kilometer. Ek purani bike pe. Do dost. Aur ek raasta jahan se pichle
3 log laute nahi.” (ANSWERS partial + raises stakes!)
 SCENE 5 → SCENE 6 TRANSITION:
 END SCENE 5: [VISUAL: Zain finds hidden compartment] NARRATION: “Aur
jab Zain ne woh darwaza khola…” (CLIFFHANGER + AUDIO continues over cut)
START SCENE 6: [VISUAL: What’s inside compartment] NARRATION: “…uski duniya badal
gayi.” (AUDIO BRIDGE complete!)

narration_rules.critical_image_vs_lastframe_decision:
## CRITICAL: IMAGE vs LASTFRAME DECISION 

    DEFAULT = NEW IMAGE (with character/object references!) 
LASTFRAME = ONLY for CONTINUOUS shots!     Lastframe is EXCEPTION, not
DEFAULT!  


### - WRONG UNDERSTANDING (What AI thinks):

“Every clip after first = use lastframe”

Clip 1.1: Image  Clip 1.2: Lastframe Clip 1.3: Lastframe Clip 1.4: Lastframe …
This is WRONG! This makes sense only for CONTINUOUS shots!


### + CORRECT UNDERSTANDING:

MOST clips = NEW IMAGE (with references attached!) ONLY truly continuous shots =
Lastframe
Clip 1.1: NEW IMAGE (wide shot haveli) Clip 1.2: NEW IMAGE (Zain walking - attach
CHAR_Zain_ref!) Clip 1.3: NEW IMAGE (close-up door - new angle!) Clip 1.4: LASTFRAME
(door opening - CONTINUES from 1.3) Clip 1.5: NEW IMAGE (inside room - new location!)
Clip 1.6: NEW IMAGE (Zain’s face reaction - attach CHAR_Zain_ref!) Clip 1.7: LASTFRAME
(Zain walks forward - CONTINUES from 1.6)

---

### WHEN TO USE WHAT:

  USE NEW IMAGE (Most clips - 70-80%):

 Different camera angle than previous clip  Different shot type (wide → medium →
close-up)  Character appears who wasn’t in previous frame  New location or
significantly different framing  Object appears that wasn’t visible before  Any cut/edit
point in cinematic terms
ALWAYS ATTACH REFERENCES:  Character visible? → Attach CHAR_[Name]ref.png
 - Specific object? → Attach OBJ[Name]_ref.png  Multiple characters? → Attach ALL
character refs!  NO EXCEPTIONS!
  USE LASTFRAME (Only continuous shots - 20-30%):

 SAME camera angle continuing  SAME framing, just action progressing  Character
doing continuous motion (walking, reaching)  Door opening that started in previous clip
 Smooth camera movement continuing
Examples of CONTINUOUS shots:  Clip 3.4: Zain reaches for book  Clip 3.5:
LASTFRAME - Hand grabs book (continues reach) |  Clip 5.2: Door starts opening 
Clip 5.3: LASTFRAME - Door fully opens (continues motion) |  Clip 7.1: Zain walking
down corridor  Clip 7.2: LASTFRAME - Continues walking (same shot)

---

### SCENE EXAMPLE - Correct Approach:

 SCENE 3: Zain Discovers the Book (6 clips)
Clip 3.1: Wide shot - study room  TYPE: NEW IMAGE  ATTACH: None
(environment only)  WHY: Establishing shot, new angle
Clip 3.2: Medium shot - Zain enters room  TYPE: NEW IMAGE ← Not lastframe! 
ATTACH: CHAR_[Hero]_Protagonist_ref.png  WHY: Character appears, different framing
Clip 3.3: Close-up - Zain’s face looking around  TYPE: NEW IMAGE ← Not lastframe!
 - ATTACH: CHAR_[Hero]_Protagonist_ref.png  WHY: Different shot type (medium →
close-up)
Clip 3.4: Medium shot - Zain approaches bookshelf  TYPE: NEW IMAGE ← Not
lastframe!  ATTACH: CHAR_[Hero]_Protagonist_ref.png  WHY: Different angle, new
framing

Clip 3.5: Close-up - Hand reaching for book  TYPE: LASTFRAME  (Continues from 3.4)
 - ATTACH: Clip_3.4_lastframe.png  WHY: CONTINUOUS action - reach continues

Clip 3.6: Extreme close-up - Book being pulled out  TYPE: LASTFRAME  (Continues
from 3.5)  ATTACH: Clip_3.5_lastframe.png  WHY: CONTINUOUS action - pull
continues

---

### SUMMARY:

    70-80% clips: NEW IMAGE (always attach references!)   20-30%
clips: LASTFRAME (only for continuous shots)     When in doubt: USE NEW IMAGE
WITH REFERENCES!

narration_rules.character_consistency_lock_critical_for:
##  CHARACTER CONSISTENCY LOCK (CRITICAL FOR VIDEO!)

    #1 REASON FOR BAD AI VIDEO: CHARACTER MORPHING! 
 If you don’t LOCK character details in video prompt,   Grok will CHANGE face,
clothes, proportions mid-clip!     EVERY video prompt with a character MUST have a
 CHARACTER LOCK section!  

### CHARACTER LOCK CHECKLIST (Include in EVERY video prompt!):

CHARACTER LOCK FOR [Name]:  FACE: [beard type/length, skin tone, expression]
 - HEAD: [hair/cap description, color, position]  CLOTHING: [each visible layer with
color]  POSTURE: [body angle, stance]  “MUST remain consistent throughout - no
morphing”

### WHY CHARACTER LOCK MATTERS:

 - WITHOUT CHARACTER LOCK:
VIDEO PROMPT: “The elderly man walks forward 3 steps while holding the book.”
WHAT HAPPENS:  Frame 1: Face clear, beard visible  Frame 30: Face darker,
features shifting  Frame 60: Beard shape different  Frame 90: Clothes color
slightly changed  Frame 120: Proportions distorted  Frame 144: Character looks
like different person!  RESULT: Unusable “melting” video!
 + WITH CHARACTER LOCK:
VIDEO PROMPT: “The elderly man walks forward 3 steps while holding the book.
CHARACTER LOCK:
 • FACE: Grey-white full beard (3 inches), weathered brown skin, fearful expression
 with furrowed brow
 • HEAD: Patterned Kashmiri cap (cream/brown geometric), firmly on head at slight
 forward tilt
 • CLOTHING: Grey-brown woolen shawl over dark brown kurta
 • POSTURE: Upright, leaning forward 10-15 degrees while walking
MUST remain consistent throughout - no morphing allowed.“
WHAT HAPPENS:  Frame 1: Character matches description  Frame 30: Character
still matches  Frame 60: Character still matches  Frame 90: Character still matches
 - Frame 144: Character STILL matches!  RESULT: Consistent, professional video!

 1. SETTING/LOCATION:  Specific place (not just “cave” but “narrow rocky alcove”)
 - Time period (1840s, present day, etc.)  Time of day (night, golden hour,

 Material/texture (brass, leather, rough stone)

 5. WHAT TO EXCLUDE:  Don’t say “NO fog” - instead just don’t mention fog 
 State what IS there, not what ISN’T  Exception: “No readable text” is okay for

 6. TECHNICAL:  “16:9, photorealistic, cinematic, ultra-detailed”


**- vs + IMAGE PROMPT COMPARISON:**

above three dots arranged in a triangle. Fresh scratch marks. Hands medium brown, rough.
Lighting: warm lantern from LEFT, cool moonlight from RIGHT.

Carving NOW or ALREADY CARVED?  “Hands” = Which hand holds chisel? Which

OBJECT STATE: The rock surface is BLANK - no carving marks yet. The chisel tip is

SPATIAL: The hand is approximately 18 inches from camera. The rock wall fills the
background entirely.
LIGHTING:
 • Primary: Warm orange lantern light from frame-LEFT (60%)
 • Secondary: Cool blue moonlight spill from frame-RIGHT (40%)
 • Creates dramatic shadow of hand on rock surface
 • High contrast between lit and shadow areas
ATMOSPHERE: Clean air, no fog or haze. A few tiny dust particles visible in the lantern light
beam.
16:9, photorealistic, cinematic, ultra-detailed macro feel.
WHAT’S BETTER:  Exact framing: “Close-up, 80% of frame”  Exact hand: “RIGHT
hand grips chisel”  Exact object: “4 inches long, dark metal”  Exact state: “BLANK -
no carving marks yet”  Exact lighting: “60% warm LEFT, 40% cool RIGHT”  Clear
what IS there (not what isn’t)  Gemini knows EXACTLY what to create!


 Save as: `Clip_[X.X]_image.png`


GROK VIDEO PROMPT SYSTEM (COMPLETE OVERHAUL!)
THIS SECTION REPLACES ALL PREVIOUS VIDEO PROMPT GUIDANCE
Based on: Grok Imagine official guide, community testing,
Aurora engine documentation, and REAL user feedback.
Grok Image-to-Video = Our PRIMARY video generation tool


HOW GROK IMAGE-TO-VIDEO WORKS:
1. You UPLOAD a generated frame image
2. You write a MOTION PROMPT describing what happens
3. Grok ANIMATES the image for 6-15 seconds
4. The image IS the first frame — Grok brings it to life

CRITICAL UNDERSTANDING:
Grok ALREADY HAS the scene from the image!
It can SEE: environment, characters, objects, lighting
It DOES NOT NEED: re-description of static elements
Your prompt should ONLY describe:
→ WHAT MOVES (subject + action)
→ HOW IT MOVES (intensity, speed, direction)
→ HOW CAMERA MOVES (pan, zoom, drift)
→ WHAT WE HEAR (audio, dialogue, SFX)
DO NOT re-describe what's already visible in the image!
Grok will expand your prompt based on what it SEES.


GROK VIDEO PROMPT GOLDEN FORMULA:
[Subject Feature] + [Action with Intensity Adverb]
+ [Camera Movement] + [Audio/Atmosphere]
KEEP IT: 50-150 words MAX for video prompts!
UNDER 200 words ALWAYS!
First 20-30 words = MOST IMPORTANT (Grok prioritizes)

WHY SHORT PROMPTS WIN:
- Grok's Aurora engine EXPANDS short prompts intelligently
- Long prompts OVERLOAD the model → ignores details
- Grok reads the IMAGE for static info — you add MOTION only
- 50-150 word prompts = BEST results (confirmed by testing)

YOUR CURRENT PROBLEM — OVER-DESCRIPTION:
Your current prompts are 300-500 words with:
- 10+ lines re-describing what's already in the image
- Inch-level measurements Grok can't process
- 7-layer acting system too complex for video AI
- Timestamp beats (0-2s, 2-4s) Grok can't follow precisely
- Extensive LOCK sections that don't affect video output

THE FIX — MOTION-FOCUSED, SHORT, INTENSE:
50-150 words focusing ONLY on what CHANGES.


GROK VIDEO PROMPT STRUCTURE (NEW!):

Every video prompt follows this 5-LAYER structure:

LAYER 1: SUBJECT + MAIN ACTION (First 20-30 words!)
"The young man in indigo coat reaches powerfully toward 
the wooden chest, his expression intense and urgent."

LAYER 2: SECONDARY MOTION + ENVIRONMENT LIFE
"Wind whips through the narrow mountain pass, torch flames 
bend sharply to the right, loose dust lifts from the stone path."

LAYER 3: CAMERA MOVEMENT
"Slow cinematic push-in toward the subject, handheld 
tension feel, slight drift."

LAYER 4: PHYSICAL REALISM (body physics!)
"His coat fabric flutters in the wind, chest rises with 
heavy breathing, weight shifts to his front foot."

LAYER 5: AUDIO DIRECTION
"Audio: howling mountain wind, distant arrow whistles, 
crackling torch fire, no music."


THE </narration_rules>

storytelling_rules.critical_proper_story_crafting_do:
### CRITICAL: Proper Story Crafting (DO NOT SKIP THIS)

**THE BIGGEST MISTAKE AI MAKES:**
Writing generic openings like:
"Do dost apni nayi kahani ke liye tayar ho rahe the..."
"Yeh unki dosti aur junoon ka imtehaan tha..."
"Safar shuru ho raha hai..."

**THIS IS GARBAGE STORYTELLING!**
- No context - WHO are these people?
- No backstory - WHY are they doing this?
- No emotional hook - WHY should viewer CARE?
- No setup - WHAT is the situation?

---

### + CORRECT WAY: Build Foundation FIRST
**Before ANY action, viewer MUST know:**
1. WHO is the main character? (Name, personality, situation)
2. WHAT is their world? (Location, atmosphere, context)
3. WHY is this moment important? (Motivation, stakes)
4. WHAT happened before? (Backstory that matters)

---

### PROPER STORY STRUCTURE:

**PART 1: OPENING HOOK (8-15 seconds)**
- Pure CINEMATIC VISUALS only
- NO narration yet
- Establish MOOD and LOCATION
- Let viewer absorb the atmosphere
- Example: Old house exterior, golden light, dust floating, silence...

**PART 2: WORLD BUILDING NARRATION (30-60 seconds)**
- NOW start narration
- Introduce the WORLD first, then characters
- Give CONTEXT and BACKSTORY
- Make viewer UNDERSTAND and CARE

**EXAMPLE of PROPER opening narration:**

“Faisalabad ke is purane mohalle mein ek haveli thi - jise log ‘Kitaabon wala ghar’ kehte the.
Is ghar mein rehte the Danish sahab. Ek aisa insaan jisne apni poori zindagi ilm ki talaash
mein guzaari. Kitabein padhna, purani dastaavez dhundna, raazon ko samajhna - yeh unka
junoon tha.
Logon ka kehna tha ke Danish sahab ke paas aisi kitabein hain jo duniya mein kahin nahi
milteen. Kuch log to yahan tak kehte the ke un kitaabon mein aisa ilm hai jo insaan ki
samajh se pare hai.
Danish sahab ka ek pota tha - Zain. Bachpan se Dada se mohabbat thi. Har garmi ki chutti
yahan aata, Dada ke saath waqt guzaarta. Lekin Dada ne kabhi un kitaabon ko Zain ke haath
nahi lagane dia.
‘Beta, pehle taleem mukammal karo’ - Dada hamesha kehte.
Aur Zain ne sun li. Lahore chala gaya, university mein admission liya.
Lekin ab… Danish sahab is duniya mein nahi rahe. Aur 2 saal baad, Zain pehli baar wapas aa
raha hai. Ab woh kitabein… uski hain.“

**SEE THE DIFFERENCE?**
- We know WHO Danish sahab was
- We know his PASSION and REPUTATION
- We know WHO Zain is and his CONNECTION
- We know WHY he stayed away
- We know WHY he's coming back NOW
- Viewer is now INVESTED

**PART 3: CHARACTER INTRODUCTION (Natural Entry)**
- After backstory, introduce character VISUALLY
- Entry should feel NATURAL (arriving, opening door, etc.)
- Show their PERSONALITY through actions
- First dialogue should reveal character

**PART 4: DIALOGUE-DRIVEN STORY**
- Once setup is complete, CHARACTERS take over
- Narration becomes MINIMAL (only for time jumps/context)
- Dialogues drive plot forward
- Actions speak louder than narration

---

### SCENE-BY-SCENE REQUIREMENTS:

**Scene 1 MUST establish:**
- Main character(s) backstory
- The world/setting context
- WHY this story is happening NOW
- Emotional connection with viewer

**Scene 2 onwards:**
- Build on established foundation
- Introduce new elements gradually
- Let characters drive the story
- Use narration sparingly

---

### STRICT RULES:

1. **NEVER start with action without context**
 - "Do dost safar par nikal rahe the..."
 - + First tell us WHO they are, WHY they're traveling

2. **NEVER use generic motivations**
 - "Yeh unki dosti ka imtehaan tha"
 - + Give SPECIFIC reason (finding grandfather's treasure, solving
mystery, etc.)

3. **ALWAYS answer these before Scene 1 ends:**
 - Who is the protagonist?
 - What do they want?
 - Why do they want it?
 - What's stopping them?
 - Why should we care?

4. **OPENING NARRATION must be MINIMUM 30-45 seconds**
 - This is NOT optional
 - This builds the FOUNDATION
 - Without this, story has no weight

5. **First character dialogue should NOT be generic**
 - "Chalo safar shuru karte hain"
 - + Something that reveals character/situation

---

### PACING GUIDE:

For a 10-minute video:
- Opening Hook: 10-15 seconds (1-2 clips)
- Backstory/Setup Narration: 45-60 seconds (8-10 clips)
- Character Introduction: 30-45 seconds (5-7 clips)
- Rising Action: 3-4 minutes (dialogue-driven)
- Midpoint: 1 minute (twist/revelation)
- Climax Build: 2-3 minutes
- Climax: 1-2 minutes
- Resolution: 30-60 seconds

---

### SELF-CHECK BEFORE WRITING SCENES:

Ask yourself:
Does viewer know WHO the main character is?
Does viewer know WHY this story matters?
Does viewer know WHAT happened before?
Is there emotional investment built?
Would I watch this if I knew nothing?

If ANY answer is NO → Rewrite the opening!
storytelling_rules.critical_preventing_appearing_out_of:
### CRITICAL: Preventing "Appearing Out of Nowhere" Problem

**THE PROBLEM:**
When you write a video prompt that introduces a NEW element (object, detail,
location) that wasn't visible in the last frame, Grok will make it APPEAR
suddenly - like materializing from thin air or emerging from a wall.

**REAL EXAMPLE OF THE PROBLEM:**

Clip 1.3 ends with: “Wide view of study room, bookshelves on walls…” Clip 1.4 prompt:
“Extreme close-up of locked brass cage with old books…”
RESULT: The brass cage APPEARS/MATERIALIZES because it wasn’t in the previous frame.
Looks like magic trick, breaks immersion!

---

### TWO SOLUTIONS:

**SOLUTION 1: Element Must Be VISIBLE in Previous Frame**

If you want to zoom into or focus on something in the next clip, it MUST be
visible (even small/partial) in the current clip's last frame.

CORRECT - Element seeded in previous clip:
Clip 1.3 VIDEO PROMPT ending: “The shot ends with: Wide view of entire study room -
bookshelves reaching ceiling on three walls. In the CENTER SHELF, a small GLINT OF
BRASS is visible - an ornate locked section holding special books, barely noticeable but
present in frame…”
Clip 1.4 VIDEO PROMPT: “Attach: Clip_1.3_lastframe.png
Camera pushes in toward the brass glint visible in the center shelf from the previous frame.
As we get closer, the details reveal - an ornate locked brass cage built into the mahogany
shelving, holding five ancient leather-bound books…“

**SOLUTION 2: Camera DISCOVERS Through Continuous Movement**

Instead of cutting to a new element, the camera TRAVELS and DISCOVERS it
naturally.

CORRECT - Discovery through movement:
Clip 1.4 VIDEO PROMPT: “Attach: Clip_1.3_lastframe.png
Camera continues its slow movement through the study room from previous position. It
TRAVELS smoothly along the bookshelf wall, PASSING rows of dusty books, until it
DISCOVERS something different - a section protected by an ornate brass cage. Camera
SETTLES on this discovery, slowly pushing in to reveal the locked cage holding five ancient
books inside. The movement feels like natural exploration, not a sudden cut…“
---

### ELEMENT INTRODUCTION RULES:

| Scenario | Wrong Approach - | Correct Approach + |
|----------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Zoom to detail | "Close-up of [new object]" | Seed object in previous
frame's ending, then zoom |
| New object in scene | "A [object] is visible" | Camera discovers through
movement OR object was visible (small) in last frame |
| Character enters | "Character standing in room" | Previous frame shows
door, this frame shows door opening and character entering |
| Reveal hidden item | "The hidden box appears" | Character's hand moves
something, revealing the box underneath |

---

### LAST FRAME DESCRIPTION RULES:

When writing "The shot ends with:", you MUST include:

1. **Everything currently visible** - All major elements in frame
2. **Seeds for next clip** - Any element you'll focus on next (even if small)
3. **Camera position** - Where is camera now? (for movement continuity)
4. **Character positions** - If any characters, where are they?

**Example - Proper Last Frame Description:**

The shot ends with: Wide view of the magnificent study room - dark mahogany
bookshelves reaching 20-foot ceiling on three walls, thousands of dusty leather-bound
books stacked chaotically, golden sunlight streaming through tall arched windows on the
right creating diagonal light beams with floating dust particles, antique brass chandelier
hanging from ornate ceiling, massive carved desk visible center-left with scattered papers,
[SEED FOR NEXT CLIP:] and in the CENTER BOOKSHELF at eye level, a GLINT OF BRASS is
barely visible - some kind of locked section different from the regular shelves. Camera
position: Wide angle from near the entrance, facing into room.

---

### TRANSITION SMOOTHNESS CHECKLIST:

Before writing each clip, verify:

Is the main subject of this clip VISIBLE in the previous clip's last
frame?
If introducing new element, is it SEEDED (visible, even small) in previous
frame?
If new element wasn't seeded, does camera DISCOVER it through MOVEMENT?
Does the camera movement feel CONTINUOUS from previous clip?
Would these two clips feel like ONE SMOOTH SHOT if played together?

**If ANY answer is NO:**
- Either go back and ADD the element to previous clip's last frame
description
- Or rewrite current clip to show DISCOVERY through camera movement
- Or add a TRANSITION CLIP between them

---

### COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:

WRONG: “Extreme close-up of the ancient map on the desk” (If map wasn’t visible in
last frame, it will APPEAR magically)

CORRECT: Previous clip ends with “desk visible with scattered papers, a YELLOWED
CORNER of something peeking from under the documents…” Next clip: “Camera pushes
toward the desk, character’s hand moves the papers aside, REVEALING an ancient folded
map underneath…”


WRONG: “Close-up of character’s emotional face” (If character wasn’t in frame, face will
appear from nowhere)

CORRECT: Previous clip ends with “character visible in doorway…” Next clip: “Camera
moves toward character, pushing in from medium to close-up, revealing the emotion
building on their face…”


WRONG: “A locked brass cage in the bookshelf holds special books” (Cage appears out
of the wall/shelf magically)

CORRECT: Previous clip ends with “bookshelves visible, and among them a GLINT of
brass catches the light - something different…” Next clip: “Camera dollies toward the brass
glint, revealing it to be an ornate locked cage protecting ancient books inside…”

---
storytelling_rules.critical_cliptoclip_sync_camera_continui:
### CRITICAL: Clip-to-Clip Sync & Camera Continuity

**ALL clips within a scene MUST flow seamlessly together!**

---

the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read:
### THE BIGGEST CONTINUITY MISTAKE (READ CAREFULLY!)

**AI often writes clips that are IMPOSSIBLE to connect!**

**REAL EXAMPLE OF FAILURE:**

Clip 1.1: Extreme close-up of book spine ENDS WITH: “Gold lettering filling the frame, light
overwhelming”
Clip 1.2: Wide shot of entire library room from floor level STARTS WITH: “Low-angle wide
shot of enormous study room…”

THIS IS IMPOSSIBLE!
 • Camera was on BOOK SPINE (extreme close-up)
 • Next clip starts from FLOOR looking at ENTIRE ROOM
 • Camera cannot TELEPORT! This creates jarring, broken video!

**ANOTHER FAILURE EXAMPLE:**

Clip 1.2: ENDS WITH: “Focus on high ceiling carvings, top of bookshelves” Clip 1.3: STARTS
WITH: “Medium shot of antique globe near window”

IMPOSSIBLE!
 • Camera was looking at CEILING
 • Now suddenly looking at GLOBE near window?
 • The globe wasn’t even in the previous frame!

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.the_golden_rule_last_frame:
###  THE GOLDEN RULE: Last Frame = Next Frame Start

**What camera SEES at the END of Clip X = What camera SEES at the START of
Clip X+1**

This is NON-NEGOTIABLE. Video AI will use your last frame as reference. If
your next clip describes something completely different, the video will have
jarring jumps.

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.last_frame_reality_check_mandatory:
### LAST FRAME REALITY CHECK (MANDATORY!)

Before writing EVERY clip, you MUST ask:

**Question 1:** "If I FREEZE the previous clip at exactly 6 seconds, what is
VISIBLE in that frame?"
- What objects are in frame?
- What is the camera angle?
- What is the camera distance (close-up, medium, wide)?
- What is visible in center, left, right of frame?

**Question 2:** "Can my next clip's STARTING point realistically BEGIN from
that frozen frame?"
- If previous ended on CEILING → Next cannot start on FLOOR
- If previous ended on BOOK CLOSE-UP → Next cannot start on WIDE ROOM
- If previous ended looking LEFT → Next cannot suddenly be looking RIGHT

**If the answer to Question 2 is NO → You MUST fix it:**
- Anchor Image Method: Change the previous clip's ending
- Anchor Image Method: Change the current clip's starting
- Option C: Generate NEW IMAGE for current clip
- Option D: Add a TRANSITION clip between them

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.correct_flow_examples:
### CORRECT FLOW EXAMPLES:

**EXAMPLE 1 - Close-up to Wide (CORRECT WAY):**

WRONG: Clip 1.1: Extreme close-up of book spine Ends: Book spine filling frame Clip
1.2: Wide shot of entire room → IMPOSSIBLE JUMP!

CORRECT: Clip 1.1: Extreme close-up of book spine Ends: Book spine in center, starting
to pull back Clip 1.2: Camera continues pulling back, revealing shelf Ends: Multiple books
visible, pulling back more Clip 1.3: Camera continues pulling back, revealing room section
Ends: Quarter of room visible Clip 1.4: Camera continues, now wide shot of room →
SMOOTH TRANSITION through 4 clips!
OR (using new image):
Clip 1.1: Extreme close-up of book spine (OPENING HOOK) Ends: Gold lettering in bright
light
Clip 1.2: Generate NEW IMAGE - Different angle, new starting point Image: Wide shot of
library room Video: Camera establishes the space → Clean cut (acceptable for opening
montage)

**EXAMPLE 2 - Ceiling to Globe (CORRECT WAY):**

WRONG: Clip 1.2: Ends on ceiling carvings Clip 1.3: Shows globe near window → Globe
wasn’t visible! Where did it come from?
CORRECT (Anchor Image Method - Globe must be visible): Clip 1.2: Camera pans up ceiling, then
begins to pan DOWN Ends: Camera descending, globe VISIBLE in lower frame
Clip 1.3: Camera continues descending, settling on globe → Globe was already IN FRAME,
now we focus on it!

CORRECT (Anchor Image Method - Generate new image): Clip 1.2: Ends on ceiling
Clip 1.3: Generate NEW IMAGE - Globe near window Note: This is a CUT, not continuous
motion Acceptable for atmospheric montage sequences

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.continuous_vs_cut_when_each:
### CONTINUOUS vs CUT - When Each is Appropriate:

**CONTINUOUS MOTION (clips flow into each other):**
- Use for: Story moments, character actions, reveals, tension building
- Requires: Perfect last frame → first frame match
- Feels: Cinematic, immersive, professional

**CUT (new image, new angle):**
- Use for: Montage sequences, establishing different details, time jumps
- Requires: Generate NEW IMAGE for the clip
- Feels: Editorial, fast-paced, can be atmospheric
- Note: Even cuts should have THEMATIC connection (same location, similar
lighting)

**OPENING SEQUENCE (Clips 1.1-1.4 typically):**
- Often uses CUTS between different details
- Book spine → Room wide → Globe → Desk (all CUTS)
- BUT each needs NEW IMAGE generation, not last frame!
- This is MONTAGE style, acceptable for establishing atmosphere

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.scene_opening_strategy_important:
### SCENE OPENING STRATEGY (IMPORTANT!):

**For atmospheric opening sequences (like library reveal):**

MONTAGE APPROACH (cuts between details): Clip 1.1: NEW IMAGE - Book spine close-up
(Hook) Clip 1.2: NEW IMAGE - Wide room shot (Scale) Clip 1.3: NEW IMAGE - Globe detail
(World building) Clip 1.4: NEW IMAGE - Desk with papers (Character hint) Clip 1.5: Start
using last frames - Now continuous motion begins
Each clip is its own IMAGE + VIDEO. These are CUTS, not continuous motion. This is
acceptable for opening montage.
CONTINUOUS APPROACH (one flowing shot): Clip 1.1: Wide exterior of haveli Clip 1.2:
Camera pushes toward door (continuous) Clip 1.3: Camera enters doorway (continuous)
Clip 1.4: Camera reveals hallway (continuous) Clip 1.5: Camera enters study room
(continuous) Clip 1.6: Camera reveals full room (continuous)
All clips use last frame of previous. One “virtual steadicam” shot through space. Very
cinematic but requires more clips.

**DECIDE your approach BEFORE writing clips and STICK to it!**

the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.camera_position_tracking:
### CAMERA POSITION TRACKING:

For every clip, mentally track:

Clip 1.1: Camera at [POSITION A] looking at [SUBJECT A] Ends at: [POSITION A’] looking at
[SUBJECT A’]
Clip 1.2: Camera MUST start at [POSITION A’] looking at [SUBJECT A’] Then moves to:
[POSITION B] looking at [SUBJECT B]
Clip 1.3: Camera MUST start at [POSITION B] looking at [SUBJECT B] …and so on

the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.cinematic_camera_shots_guide_use:
###  CINEMATIC CAMERA SHOTS GUIDE (USE THESE!)

**Professional videos use VARIETY of camera shots and movements. Don't just
use basic pans and static shots - use the FULL cinematic toolkit!**

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.drone_aerial_shots_very_cinematic:
### DRONE / AERIAL SHOTS (Very Cinematic!)

**When to Use Drone Shots:**
- Opening establishing shots (city, landscape, building)
- Scene transitions (moving between locations)
- Climax moments (showing scale, vastness)
- Chase/travel sequences
- Revealing hidden locations
- Ending/closing shots

**Types of Drone Shots:**
| Shot Name | Description | Best For |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| **Bird's Eye** | Directly overhead, looking straight down | Maps, patterns,
scale |
| **High Angle Aerial** | High up but angled (45°) toward subject |
Establishing cities, buildings |
| **Drone Push-In** | Flying forward toward subject | Approaching location,
reveal |
| **Drone Pull-Out** | Flying backward away from subject | Ending scenes,
showing isolation |
| **Drone Orbit** | Circling around subject | Hero shots, monuments, climax |
| **Drone Rise/Descend** | Vertical movement up or down | Reveal from ground,
descent to character |
| **Drone Flyover** | Flying over landscape/location | Travel, transition,
establishing |
| **Drone Follow** | Following subject from above | Chase, journey, character
movement |
| **Drone Tracking** | Moving parallel to subject | Vehicles, walking, action
|
| **Crane Up to Drone** | Starting low, rising to aerial view | Epic reveals,
climax moments |

**Drone Shot Examples for Prompts:**

OPENING - City Establishing: “Aerial drone shot high above Faisalabad city at golden hour.
Camera slowly descends while pushing forward toward the old district, revealing the
contrast between modern buildings and ancient mohalla. The haveli becomes visible
among the old structures as drone continues descending.”
CLIMAX - Scale Reveal: “Dramatic drone pullback starting close to Zain standing at the cliff
edge, then rapidly pulling back and rising to reveal the vast Himalayan landscape stretching
endlessly - snow-capped peaks, deep valleys, the ancient monastery below. The scale
emphasizes how small Zain is against this immense quest.”
TRANSITION - Location Change: “Aerial drone flyover across the landscape - starting over
Faisalabad’s urban sprawl, transitioning over fields and highways, ending as mountains
appear on the horizon - suggesting the journey ahead.”
ENDING - Isolation: “Final drone shot slowly rising and pulling away from the haveli, Zain
visible as a tiny figure in the courtyard. The camera continues rising until the entire
neighborhood is visible, then the whole district, emphasizing the weight of his solitary
mission.”

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.crane_shots_professional_look:
### CRANE SHOTS (Professional Look!)

**When to Use Crane Shots:**
- Dramatic reveals (rising to show something)
- Character power moments (rising with character)
- Transitions within a location
- Following vertical movement (stairs, climbing)
- Emotional climax moments

**Types of Crane Shots:**

| Shot Name | Description | Best For |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| **Crane Up** | Camera rises vertically | Reveal, power, victory |
| **Crane Down** | Camera descends vertically | Arrival, intimacy, focus |
| **Crane + Push** | Rising while moving forward | Dynamic reveal |
| **Crane + Pull** | Rising while moving backward | Departure, ending |
| **Crane Arc** | Rising in curved path | Dramatic character moment |
| **Boom Up** | Quick vertical rise | Sudden reveal, surprise |
| **Jib Sweep** | Sweeping horizontal + vertical | Establishing, grandeur |

**Crane Shot Examples for Prompts:**

CHARACTER POWER MOMENT: “Crane shot starting at ground level on Zain’s feet, slowly
rising up his body as he stands with determination, continuing up to reveal his face against
the dramatic sky - a hero shot showing his resolve.”
ROOM REVEAL: “Crane shot starting at floor level near the Persian rug, slowly rising and
tilting up to reveal the towering bookshelves, continuing up toward the ornate ceiling -
emphasizing the grand scale of the study.”
DRAMATIC MOMENT: “Crane descends from high angle toward Zain kneeling at his
grandfather’s grave, slowly moving down and in until we’re at eye level with his grief-
stricken face - the descent matching his emotional weight.”

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.steadicam_gimbal_shots_smooth_following:
### STEADICAM / GIMBAL SHOTS (Smooth Following)

**When to Use:**
- Following characters through spaces
- Long continuous takes
- Walking and talking scenes
- Exploration sequences
- Smooth movement through locations

**Types:**

| Shot Name | Description | Best For |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| **Follow Shot** | Camera follows behind character | Journey, exploration |
| **Lead Shot** | Camera in front, facing character | Conversation, emotion |
| **Side Track** | Moving alongside character | Walking, dialogue |
| **360° Walk Around** | Orbiting around subject on ground | Intense moment,
confrontation |
| **Push Through** | Moving through doorways, spaces | Entering new location
|

**Examples:**

EXPLORATION: “Steadicam follows behind Zain as he walks slowly through the dark haveli
corridor, camera maintaining consistent distance, moving smoothly as he pushes open the
study door and steps inside - one continuous movement.”
EMOTIONAL MOMENT: “Gimbal shot slowly orbiting around Zain as he stands in the center
of the study, 180-degree arc from his back to his tear-streaked face, maintaining focus as
the room spins around him - disorientation matching his emotion.”

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.dolly_shots_controlled_movement:
### DOLLY SHOTS (Controlled Movement)

**Types:**

| Shot Name | Description | Best For |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| **Dolly In** | Moving toward subject | Increasing intensity, focus |
| **Dolly Out** | Moving away from subject | Reveal, isolation, ending |
| **Dolly Across** | Moving parallel to subject | Following action, pan
alternative |
| **Dolly + Zoom (Vertigo)** | Dolly out while zooming in | Disorientation,
realization |

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.specialized_cinematic_shots:
### SPECIALIZED CINEMATIC SHOTS

| Shot Name | Description | Best For |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| **Dutch Angle** | Camera tilted on axis | Unease, tension, instability |
| **Low Angle** | Camera below subject, looking up | Power, intimidation,
grandeur |
| **High Angle** | Camera above, looking down | Vulnerability, overview |
| **POV Shot** | Camera shows character's view | Immersion, discovery |
| **Over-the-Shoulder** | Camera behind one character | Dialogue,
confrontation |
| **Insert/Cutaway** | Close detail shot | Important objects, clues |
| **Whip Pan** | Very fast pan | Transition, surprise |
| **Rack Focus** | Focus shifts foreground to background | Reveal, connection
|
| **Slow Motion** | Slowed footage | Dramatic moment, impact |

the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.when_to_use_which_shot:
### WHEN TO USE WHICH SHOT:

| Story Moment | Recommended Shots |
|--------------|-------------------|
| **Opening/Establishing** | Drone aerial, Crane down, Wide static |

the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.shot_variety_rule:

(horizontal, focus) Clip 5: Static close-up on object (rest, detail) Clip 6: Low angle looking
up at bookshelves (perspective) (DYNAMIC! Each shot different!)

the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.color_consistency_anchoring_very_importa:
### COLOR CONSISTENCY ANCHORING (VERY IMPORTANT!)

**THE PROBLEM:**
When using last frame as reference, Grok often changes:
- Color temperature (warmer/cooler)
- Brightness levels
- Contrast intensity
- Shadow depth
- Highlight intensity

**Result:** Clips that should be continuous have SUDDEN color jumps!

**EXAMPLE OF THE PROBLEM:**

Clip A last frame: Soft blue-tinted snow, subtle light beams, cooler tone Clip B first frame:
Warmer golden snow, stronger light beams, higher contrast
Even though it’s the same scene, the color shift creates a jarring cut!
---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.solution_color_anchoring_in_every:
### SOLUTION: Color Anchoring in Every Prompt

**Add EXPLICIT color matching instructions in every video prompt:**

**METHOD 1: Reference the Attached Image Colors**

VIDEO PROMPT must include:
“CRITICAL COLOR MATCHING: The color grading, brightness, contrast, and overall tone
must EXACTLY MATCH the attached reference image. Do not shift warmer or cooler. Do not
increase or decrease contrast. Maintain the identical visual feel - as if this is a continuous
shot from the same camera with the same settings.”

**METHOD 2: Specify Exact Color Values**

“COLOR ANCHORING:
 • Color temperature: Cool blue-hour tones (as in attached image)
 • Snow color: Blue-grey with subtle warm highlights ONLY where direct sunlight hits
 • Sky gradient: Deep blue at top, soft orange at horizon
 • Shadow density: Medium-deep, matching attached image exactly
 • Highlight intensity: Soft, not blown out
 • Overall exposure: Slightly underexposed, moody
 • Contrast level: Medium-high, matching reference
DO NOT deviate from these values. This must look like a continuous shot from the attached
frame.“

**METHOD 3: Include Color Consistency Statement**

Add this to EVERY video prompt that uses lastframe:

“ CONTINUITY REQUIREMENT: This clip must have ZERO color shift from the attached
reference image. Match exactly:
 • Same color temperature
 • Same brightness level
 • Same contrast ratio
 • Same shadow depth
 • Same highlight intensity
 • Same overall mood/tone
The transition between clips must be INVISIBLE - as if one continuous recording.“

the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.no_transitions_no_morphing_rule:
### NO TRANSITIONS / NO MORPHING RULE (CRITICAL!)

**THE PROBLEM:**
Grok sometimes creates unwanted transitions within a single clip:
- Fade to different scene
- Morph/dissolve to different location
- Cross-fade between two different images
- Scene changes mid-clip

**This creates jarring, unprofessional results where buildings/locations
CHANGE during the clip!**

**SOLUTION: Add explicit NO TRANSITION statement to EVERY prompt:**

“ SINGLE CONTINUOUS SHOT:
 • This is ONE unbroken shot - NO cuts, NO fades, NO transitions
 • NO morphing or dissolving to different scene
 • The location/building remains EXACTLY the same throughout
 • NO cross-fades or scene changes within this clip
 • Start frame and end frame show the SAME location
 • Only camera movement changes, NOT the subject matter“

**Add this to EVERY video prompt:**

CONTINUITY LOCK:
 • Same haveli/location from start to end
 • NO fade transitions
 • NO morphing to different building
 • NO scene changes within clip
 • Single continuous camera movement only

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.element_introduction_rule_critical:
### ELEMENT INTRODUCTION RULE (CRITICAL!)

**THE PROBLEM:**
AI writes prompts where NEW ELEMENTS "appear" during video that weren't in
the reference image:
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.example_1_secret_shelf_appears:
EXAMPLE 1 - Secret shelf appears from nowhere: Clip 1.4: Reference image shows
“desk with regular bookshelves” Clip 1.5: “Camera pans… an unusual ornate black iron
grille APPEARS”
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.problem_the_grille_wasnt_in:
PROBLEM: The grille wasn’t in the reference image! Grok will either:
 • Not show it at all
 • Make it “pop” into existence suddenly
 • Create weird morphing effect
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.example_2_lock_appears_in:
EXAMPLE 2 - Lock appears in close-up: Clip 1.5 ends: “Grille visible” (no lock
mentioned/visible) Clip 1.6: “Close-up showing grille AND antique dusty padlock”
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.problem_padlock_wasnt_in_previous:
PROBLEM: Padlock wasn’t in previous frame! It suddenly appears in the close-up = jarring!

---

**THE GOLDEN RULE:**

If an element will be FEATURED in a clip, it MUST be VISIBLE in the REFERENCE IMAGE
for that clip!
Grok can only animate what it can SEE in the attached image. It CANNOT reliably add new
objects that aren’t there!

---

**CORRECT APPROACH - Element Introduction:**

**Step 1: Plan the reveal BACKWARDS**
FINAL SHOT: Close-up of locked grille with padlock ↓ BEFORE THAT: Medium shot where
grille AND lock are visible ↓ BEFORE THAT: Wide shot where grille is visible (small) in
frame ↓ FIRST APPEARANCE: Generate NEW IMAGE that includes the grille

**Step 2: Generate NEW IMAGE when introducing element**

When the locked grille section will FIRST appear:
DON’T: Use previous lastframe and “pan to reveal grille” DO: Generate NEW IMAGE that
INCLUDES the grille already
IMAGE PROMPT for introducing grille: “Interior of Danish Sahab’s study, bookshelves filling
the wall. In the CENTER-LEFT of the bookshelf, there is a distinctive section: an ornate
black iron grille (about 2 feet wide) built into the shelf, with a heavy antique padlock
hanging from it. Behind the iron bars, 4-5 darker, older books are visible. The rest of the
shelves have regular books. Warm golden lighting.”

 Save as: Clip_1.5_image.png
NOW the video can feature this grille because it’s IN the image!

**Step 3: Close-up needs the element in reference**

For close-up of padlock: The REFERENCE IMAGE must show the padlock!
Either: A) Previous clip’s lastframe includes visible padlock B) Generate NEW IMAGE
showing close framing with padlock visible

WRONG: Wide shot lastframe → “dolly in to show padlock detail” (Padlock wasn’t
visible in wide shot!)

CORRECT: Medium shot lastframe WITH padlock visible → “dolly in closer to padlock”
(Padlock was already in frame, now getting closer)

---

**ELEMENT INTRODUCTION CHECKLIST:**

Before writing any clip that features a specific element:

Is this element visible in the reference image I’m attaching?
 • If NO → Generate NEW IMAGE with element included
 • If YES (but small) → Can dolly in to feature it

Is the element’s DETAIL level appropriate for the shot?
 • Wide shot: Element visible but small (no fine detail)
 • Medium shot: Element clear, some detail visible
 • Close-up: Element’s details (texture, lock, text) visible

Am I asking Grok to show details that aren’t in the reference?
 • If reference shows grille from far → Cannot suddenly show lock detail
 • Need intermediate shot or NEW IMAGE with closer framing

---

**EXAMPLES - Wrong vs Right:**

WRONG - Padlock appears from nowhere:
Clip 1.5: Reference shows bookshelf, grille visible but small Video: “Camera dollies in… the
antique padlock covered in undisturbed dust becomes prominent, its keyhole visible…”
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.problem_reference_didnt_show_padlock:
PROBLEM: Reference didn’t show padlock detail! Grok will invent a random padlock or it
will “pop” in!

CORRECT - Padlock properly introduced:
Clip 1.5: Generate NEW IMAGE - Medium shot of grille section WITH padlock clearly visible
in the image
Clip 1.6: Attach Clip_1.5_lastframe (which shows padlock) Video: “Camera dollies closer to
the padlock that’s visible in the attached image, revealing more texture and dust…”
NOW it works because padlock was IN the reference!


WRONG - Hidden compartment appears:
Clip 2.4: Reference shows desk surface Video: “Zain’s hand brushes the side and discovers a
hidden compartment with a brass latch”
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.problem_hidden_compartment_wasnt_in:
PROBLEM: Hidden compartment wasn’t in reference!

CORRECT - Hidden compartment properly shown:
Clip 2.4: Generate NEW IMAGE - Desk with visible hidden compartment (slightly open or
latch visible)
Video: “The hidden compartment visible on the desk side, Zain’s hand reaches toward the
brass latch…”

---

**THE "CAN GROK SEE IT?" TEST:**
Before every clip, ask:

“If I gave this reference image to someone with NO context, could they SEE the element I’m
about to feature?”
If NO → Generate new image WITH the element If YES → Proceed with video prompt

---

**SUMMARY - ELEMENT INTRODUCTION:**

 1. Elements CANNOT “appear” during video
 2. Everything featured must be IN the reference image
 3. Generate NEW IMAGE when introducing new elements
 4. Detail level must match: wide=small, close=detailed
 5. Use “Can Grok See It?” test before every clip

---
the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.subject_consistency_no_morphing_critical:
### SUBJECT CONSISTENCY - No Morphing! (CRITICAL!)

**THE PROBLEM:**
During a single clip, Grok often CHANGES the subject:
- Door changes color (dark → red → bright red)
- Building facade changes (windows shift, details change)
- Magical lighting appears (golden glow from nowhere)
- Objects spawn (scooters, plants appear mid-clip)
- Proportions shift

**EXAMPLE OF THE PROBLEM:**

Frame 1 (Start): Haveli with DARK door, normal lighting Frame 2 (Middle): Door now RED
with golden glow! Frame 3 (End): Door BRIGHT RED, magical light, scooter appeared!
The BUILDING ITSELF changed during the 6-second clip!

---

**SOLUTION: SUBJECT LOCK in Every Prompt**

**Add explicit SUBJECT DESCRIPTION that must NOT change:**

SUBJECT LOCK - DO NOT CHANGE:
BUILDING APPEARANCE (Must match reference exactly):  Door: Dark wooden door
with arched frame (NOT red, NOT glowing)  Facade: Weathered orange/peach colored
brick  Windows: 6 windows visible, white frames, positions as in reference 
Balconies: Two balconies on upper floor, iron railings  Decorative elements: Arched
details above windows (as shown)  Condition: Aged but maintained, some wear visible
LIGHTING (No changes):  Natural golden hour sunlight from the right  NO magical
glow, NO supernatural lighting  NO spotlight effect on door  Shadows consistent
with sun position  NO dramatic lighting changes during clip
OBJECTS IN SCENE (Only these, no additions):  Street/road in foreground  Trees
on both sides (positions as in reference)  Neighboring buildings (as shown)  NO
scooters unless in reference  NO people unless in reference  NO new
plants/objects appearing
The building, door, lighting, and objects must look IDENTICAL from first frame to last
frame. Only CAMERA POSITION changes.

---

**DOOR COLOR LOCK:**

Doors changing color is a VERY common Grok problem:

CORRECT - Lock the door appearance:
“The haveli’s main entrance has a DARK WOODEN DOOR - deep brown, almost black with
age, with a simple arched frame. This door color must remain EXACTLY the same
throughout the clip - DO NOT change to red, DO NOT add golden glow, DO NOT brighten.
The door stays dark brown from start to end.”


WRONG - Vague door description:
“Camera approaches the haveli entrance” (Grok will change door color as it gets closer!)

---

**NO MAGICAL LIGHTING:**

Grok loves to add dramatic "movie magic" lighting:

COMMON GROK BEHAVIOR:
 • Adds golden glow around doors/windows
 • Creates supernatural light sources
 • Makes subjects “glow” as camera approaches
 • Adds lens flares and light leaks
PREVENT WITH:
“LIGHTING LOCK:
 • Natural daylight only (golden hour sun from right side)
 • NO magical glow around the door
 • NO supernatural light effects
 • NO spotlight or dramatic lighting appearing
 • Light remains consistent from start to end
 • NO lens flares, NO light leaks
 • The scene looks REAL, not like a movie poster“

---

**OBJECTS SPAWN PREVENTION:**

COMMON GROK BEHAVIOR:
 • Scooters/motorcycles appear
 • Plants/pots materialize
 • People walk into frame (unwanted)
 • Cars appear in background
 • Street vendors spawn

PREVENT WITH:
“OBJECT LOCK:
 • ONLY objects visible in the attached reference may appear
 • NO new vehicles (scooters, cars, motorcycles) unless in reference
 • NO new people entering frame
 • NO new plants or objects materializing
 • If something isn’t in the reference image, it should NOT appear
 • The scene contents stay CONSTANT throughout“

---

**BUILDING MORPH PREVENTION:**

COMMON GROK BEHAVIOR:
 • Window positions shift
 • Architectural details change
 • Building proportions adjust
 • Facade color shifts
 • Different building by end of clip
PREVENT WITH:
“BUILDING LOCK (Match Reference Exactly):
 • The haveli facade must look IDENTICAL throughout
 • Same window positions, same balcony positions
 • Same decorative elements, same colors
 • NO architectural changes during clip
 • If you freeze any frame, the building should match the reference
 • The building does NOT change - only camera position changes“

---

the_biggest_continuity_mistake_read.physically_possible_camera_movements_cri:
### PHYSICALLY POSSIBLE CAMERA MOVEMENTS (CRITICAL!)

**THE PROBLEM:**
AI writes camera movements that are PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE, causing Grok to
create weird, broken clips.

**EXAMPLE OF IMPOSSIBLE MOVEMENT:**

Clip 1.1 ENDS: “Wide, HIGH-ANGLE view of haveli facade” (Camera is UP HIGH, looking
down)
Clip 1.2: “From this view, camera does dolly FORWARD toward door”

IMPOSSIBLE!
 • Camera is HIGH (looking down at building)
 • Door is at GROUND level
 • How can camera dolly FORWARD toward something BELOW it?
 • This creates confusion and weird AI output!

**CAMERA MOVEMENT PHYSICS:**

UNDERSTAND CAMERA POSITIONS:
HIGH ANGLE (camera above, looking down):  Can: Crane DOWN, Tilt down more,
Zoom in  Cannot: Dolly forward to ground-level subject  To reach ground: Must
DESCEND first
EYE LEVEL (camera at normal height):  Can: Dolly forward/back, Pan, Truck 
Natural for: Walking shots, character level  Most versatile position
LOW ANGLE (camera below, looking up):  Can: Crane UP, Tilt up more, Dolly forward
 - Cannot: Easily rise while pushing forward  Best for: Power shots, grandeur

**TRANSITION BETWEEN ANGLES:**

If Clip A ends HIGH, Clip B cannot start at GROUND level moving forward!

CORRECT SEQUENCE: Clip 1.1: Crane UP, ends HIGH looking at facade Clip 1.2: From
HIGH, slowly DESCEND while approaching Clip 1.3: Now at EYE LEVEL, dolly toward door
WRONG SEQUENCE: Clip 1.1: Crane UP, ends HIGH looking at facade
Clip 1.2: Suddenly at ground level, dolly toward door (Camera teleported!)

---

**CAMERA MOVEMENT COMPATIBILITY CHART:**

| If Clip Ends At | Next Clip Can Start With |
|-----------------|-------------------------|
| HIGH angle (above subject) | Descend, Zoom in, Hold, Tilt |
| EYE LEVEL | Dolly, Pan, Truck, Crane, Tilt |
| LOW angle (below subject) | Rise, Zoom in, Hold, Tilt |
| CLOSE-UP | Pull back, Hold, Pan across detail |
| WIDE shot | Push in, Pan, Crane, Hold |
| Moving FORWARD | Continue forward, Slow down, Stop |
| Moving UP | Continue up, Stop, Begin descent |

---

**BEFORE WRITING ANY CLIP, ASK:**

Where is camera at END of previous clip?
 • Height: High / Eye level / Low
 • Distance: Close / Medium / Wide
 • Direction: Moving or Static

Is my planned movement PHYSICALLY POSSIBLE from that position?
 • Can camera realistically do this movement?
 • Would it require teleportation?
 • Does gravity make sense?

If position change needed, do I need TRANSITION clip?
 • Add intermediate clip to reposition camera
 • Or describe the repositioning in current clip

---

**FIXING THE EXAMPLE:**

WRONG: Clip 1.1 ends: HIGH angle, looking down at facade Clip 1.2: “Dolly forward
toward the door” (impossible from high angle!)

CORRECT Anchor Image Method (Continuous descent): Clip 1.1 ends: HIGH angle view of facade Clip
1.2: “Camera begins slow descent from high position, gradually lowering while pushing
forward toward the building. By end of clip, camera is at eye level approaching the
entrance.” Clip 1.3: Now at eye level, “Dolly forward toward door”

CORRECT Anchor Image Method (Stay high, zoom): Clip 1.1 ends: HIGH angle view of facade Clip 1.2:
“Maintaining high angle, camera slowly zooms in toward the doorway below, door growing
larger in frame while keeping the aerial perspective.” (Movement matches the camera
position!)

CORRECT Option C (New image for cut): Clip 1.1 ends: HIGH angle view Clip 1.2:
Generate NEW IMAGE at eye level near door (This is a CUT, acceptable for establishing
sequence)
